note: v0.25: Taleb, legendary traders, actuarial science, weather forecasting and big data, written by five research agents and checked by five independent checkers.

concepts.name: Kappa-equivalent sample size
concepts.def: The number of observations from a fat-tailed variable needed to give a sample mean as reliable, in mean absolute deviation, as n_g Gaussian observations. Taleb reports that a Pareto with tail exponent 3 needs 543 observations to match 30 Gaussian ones, and that a kappa above .15 signals that the normal approximation is unreliable. For the engine it converts a tail diagnosis into an honest effective sample size for any backtest statistic.
concepts.formula: kappa(n0,n) = 2 - (log n - log n0) / log(M(n)/M(n0)), with M(n) = E|S_n - E(S_n)|; equivalent count n_nu = n_g^(-1/(kappa_1 - 1)) = n_g^(1/(1 - kappa_1))
concepts.aliases: n_nu, effective sample size under fat tails, gaussian-equivalent sample
concepts.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? An Operational, Pre-Asymptotic Metric for Fat-tailedness (Taleb, arXiv 1802.05495)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Eq. 1 and Eq. 7 match the formula; 543 and .15 on page.

concepts.name: MAD versus standard deviation under fat tails
concepts.def: Mean absolute deviation (MAD) is never larger than the standard deviation and equals about 0.8 of it for a normal distribution. Under fat tails the standard deviation is driven by a few squared extremes, so its estimate is unstable and the MAD/SD ratio falls well below 0.8. Taleb argues risk systems should report dispersion in MAD and treat sample standard deviation as fragile.
concepts.formula: MAD = E|X - E(X)|; MAD <= SD; for a normal distribution MAD = sqrt(2/pi) x SD, about 0.8 x SD
concepts.aliases: mean absolute deviation, mad, average absolute deviation
concepts.source_title: Average absolute deviation (Wikipedia)
concepts.originator: Classical statistics; argued for in finance by Goldstein and Taleb, 2007
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page: MAD <= SD and about 0.8 SD for a normal; sqrt(2/pi) is correct; Taleb advocacy appears only via the cited Edge reference.

concepts.name: Volatility definition confusion
concepts.def: The finding that finance professionals confuse mean absolute deviation with standard deviation and so understate volatility. In Goldstein and Taleb (2007) only 3 of 87 respondents gave the correct standard deviation, and the typical answer was 25% too low. A risk engine should compute dispersion from definitions, never from a practitioner's intuition.
concepts.aliases: we don't quite know what we are talking about when we talk about volatility
concepts.source_title: Misunderestimating Volatility (CXO Advisory, summary of Goldstein and Taleb 2007)
concepts.originator: Daniel Goldstein and Nassim Nicholas Taleb, 2007
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 3 of 87 and 25% too low on page.

concepts.name: Catastrophe principle
concepts.def: For subexponential (fat-tailed) variables the probability that a sum exceeds a large level is asymptotically the probability that the single largest term does. Large aggregate losses therefore come from one big jump rather than many small adverse moves, which is why diversification across many draws protects less than the Gaussian intuition suggests.
concepts.formula: lim_{x -> inf} P(S_n > x) / P(M_n > x) = 1, where S_n = X_1 + ... + X_n and M_n = max(X_1, ..., X_n)
concepts.aliases: single big jump, subexponential property, principle of the single big jump
concepts.source_title: Statistical Consequences of Fat Tails (Taleb, arXiv 2001.10488)
concepts.originator: Subexponential distribution theory (Chistyakov); used centrally by Taleb, 2020
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Book names the catastrophe principle and says S_n has the magnitude of M_n for subexponentials; formula correct.

concepts.name: Preasymptotics
concepts.def: The behavior of sample statistics when n is large but not asymptotic, which Taleb calls the law of medium numbers. Limit theorems may hold eventually, but under fat tails convergence is so slow that real samples sit far from the limit. For an engine built on about 1,870 monthly observations, it means tail quantities estimated from history can be preasymptotic and biased.
concepts.aliases: law of medium numbers, preasymptotic behavior, real world preasymptotics
concepts.source_title: Statistical Consequences of Fat Tails (Taleb, arXiv 2001.10488)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Section 2.2.3 Law of Medium Numbers or Preasymptotics; the engine sample note is an application.

concepts.name: Power-law tail exponent
concepts.def: The exponent alpha in a tail that decays as a power, P(X > x) = L(x) x^(-alpha) with L slowly varying. Moments of order p exist only for p < alpha, so alpha <= 2 implies infinite variance and alpha <= 1 an infinite mean; Taleb states that variables with alpha <= 1 are simply not forecastable. Its estimate decides whether averages, variances or Sharpe ratios mean anything.
concepts.formula: P(X > x) = L(x) x^(-alpha); E|X|^p < inf only if p < alpha; GPD shape xi = 1/alpha
concepts.source_title: On single point forecasts for fat tailed variables (Taleb, International Institute of Forecasters blog)
concepts.originator: Vilfredo Pareto and Benoit Mandelbrot; Taleb, 2020
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Formula correct (moments of order p exist for p < alpha, xi = 1/alpha); not forecastable line on page.

concepts.name: Karamata point
concepts.def: The threshold beyond which the slowly varying part L(x) of a power-law tail has effectively reached its constant limit. Tail fitting, for example with the Hill estimator, should use only observations beyond this point; starting below it mixes body and tail and biases alpha.
concepts.aliases: tail threshold, onset of power-law regime
concepts.source_title: Statistical Consequences of Fat Tails (Taleb, arXiv 2001.10488)
concepts.originator: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, 2020 (after Karamata's theory of regular variation)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Book: point where L(x) reaches its constant limit, dubbed the Karamata point.

concepts.name: Lindy property of tail exceedances
concepts.def: Under a power law the expected size of an exceedance grows in proportion to the threshold, while under a Gaussian the expected move beyond 4 standard deviations is only about 4 standard deviations. A large drawdown in fat-tailed data therefore predicts a larger conditional loss, not a bounded one. Taleb calls this the Lindy property.
concepts.formula: Pareto with exponent alpha > 1: E[X | X > K] = K alpha/(alpha - 1)
concepts.aliases: conditional exceedance scaling, mean excess under power laws
concepts.source_title: Statistical Consequences of Fat Tails (Taleb, arXiv 2001.10488)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Book: Gaussian beyond 4 SD about 4 SD, power law a multiple, called the Lindy property; Pareto formula K alpha/(alpha - 1) is correct.

concepts.name: Shadow mean
concepts.def: The mean implied by the fitted data-generating process rather than the sample average. For fat-tailed variables with a very large but finite upper bound, the data can suggest an infinite mean, yet the bound guarantees finite moments; Taleb and Cirillo say the sample mean is essentially useless for inference and the shadow mean is not immediately visible from the data. An engine should compare historical average losses with a model-implied shadow mean before trusting them.
concepts.formula: E[Y | Z > L*] = (H - L*) e^(alpha sigma/H) (alpha sigma/H)^alpha Gamma(1 - alpha, alpha sigma/H) + L*, with alpha = 1/xi from the GPD fit on the dual variable Z
concepts.source_title: On the shadow moments of apparently infinite-mean phenomena (Taleb and Cirillo, arXiv 1510.06731)
concepts.originator: Pasquale Cirillo and Nassim Nicholas Taleb, 2015
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Formula matches the paper; the considerably-larger-than-sample-mean finding is from the violent-conflicts paper, not this one.

concepts.name: Dual distribution transform
concepts.def: A log transformation that maps a variable with a remote but finite upper bound H into an unbounded variable, so extreme value theory can be applied and results mapped back. It lets fat-tailed bounded data (casualties, operational losses) be modeled without pretending moments are infinite.
concepts.formula: Z = phi(Y) = L - H log((H - Y)/(H - L)), with L the lower bound and H the upper bound of Y
concepts.aliases: dual variable, log-transformation to remove the upper bound
concepts.source_title: On the shadow moments of apparently infinite-mean phenomena (Taleb and Cirillo, arXiv 1510.06731)
concepts.originator: Pasquale Cirillo and Nassim Nicholas Taleb, 2015
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Formula phi(Y) = L - H log((H - Y)/(H - L)) matches the paper.

concepts.name: Fragility as left-tail vega
concepts.def: Taleb and Douady define fragility as the sensitivity of the left-tail expectation below a level K to an increase in dispersion, much as vega measures an option's sensitivity to volatility. A position is fragile when more uncertainty raises its expected tail loss, whatever the forecast of the mean. This turns fragility into a measurable quantity that does not require knowing the true distribution.
concepts.formula: xi(K, s-) = integral_{-inf}^{K} (Omega - x) f_lambda(x) dx; V = d xi / d s-, approximated by [xi(K, s- + ds) - xi(K, s- - ds)] / (2 ds), where s- is the left semi-absolute deviation around Omega
concepts.source_title: Mathematical Definition, Mapping, and Detection of (Anti)Fragility (Taleb and Douady, arXiv 1208.1189)
concepts.originator: Nassim Nicholas Taleb and Raphael Douady, 2012
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Paper defines fragility as left-tail shortfall sensitivity to s- with a vega analogy and a central finite difference; (Omega - x) sign convention is valid.

concepts.name: Second-order stress test
concepts.def: The IMF application of Taleb's fragility heuristic: run a stress test at a shock of plus and minus Delta (a multiple of the mean deviation) and measure the asymmetry of outcomes, scaled by capital or GDP. Negative H for capital (positive for debt) means losses accelerate faster than gains, which flags fragility even when the first-order stress test looks acceptable, and gives an ordinal ranking across banks or sovereigns.
concepts.formula: H = [f(x + Delta) + f(x - Delta)]/2 - f(x); the unnormalized form f(x - Delta) + f(x + Delta) - 2f(x) equals 2H; H < 0 for capital means fragile, H = 0 linear
concepts.aliases: imf fragility heuristic, h heuristic, tail nonlinearity test
concepts.source_title: A New Heuristic Measure of Fragility and Tail Risks: Application to Stress Testing (IMF WP/12/216)
concepts.originator: Taleb, Canetti, Kinda, Loukoianova and Schmieder, IMF WP/12/216, 2012
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Formula matches; H < 0 for capital fragile, positive for debt; authors in paper order.

concepts.name: Jensen gap
concepts.def: The difference between the expectation of a function and the function of the expectation. It is positive for convex functions and negative for concave ones, which is the mathematical engine behind antifragility and fragility: a concave exposure loses from volatility even with an unbiased forecast of the mean.
concepts.formula: J = E[f(X)] - f(E[X]); J >= 0 if f is convex, J <= 0 if f is concave
concepts.source_title: Jensen's inequality (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Article: proved by Jensen in 1906 and describes the gap; formula and signs correct.

concepts.name: Convexity bias
concepts.def: The gain (or loss) a nonlinear exposure earns from variability alone, named by Taleb and Douady as the effect from Jensen's inequality. To second order it equals half the curvature times the variance of the shock. It explains why concave positions (short options, leverage near limits) look fine on point forecasts yet lose on average.
concepts.formula: E[f(x + e)] - f(x) approx (1/2) f''(x) Var(e) for a small zero-mean shock e
concepts.source_title: Mathematical Definition, Mapping, and Detection of (Anti)Fragility (Taleb and Douady, arXiv 1208.1189)
concepts.originator: Nassim Nicholas Taleb and Raphael Douady, 2012
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Paper names Convexity Bias / effect from Jensen's inequality; second-order formula is correct.

concepts.name: Time average versus ensemble average
concepts.def: In a multiplicative bet that adds 50% on heads and takes 40% on tails, the ensemble expectation grows 5% per round while almost every single path shrinks about 5% per round. The two averages coincide only for ergodic processes. Sizing exposure from expected arithmetic returns rather than time-average growth overbets; the engine's CRRA and log objectives correct for this.
concepts.formula: Ensemble factor per round = 0.5 x 1.5 + 0.5 x 0.6 = 1.05; time-average factor = sqrt(1.5 x 0.6) = sqrt(0.9) approx 0.949; growth rate g = E[log(1 + r)]
concepts.aliases: ergodicity economics coin toss, time-average growth, multiplicative coin game
concepts.source_title: Ergodicity economics (Wikipedia)
concepts.originator: Ole Peters (ergodicity economics); popularized for finance by Taleb, 2017
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page: about 5% loss per round vs 5% gain in expectation; Peters 2011 and Taleb's use cited; arithmetic correct.

concepts.name: Ensemble probability versus time probability
concepts.def: Taleb's casino contrast: 100 different people each gambling once give the ensemble odds, while one person gambling 100 days in a row faces time probability, where one ruin ends the sequence. Strategies must be judged on the single path the investor actually lives.
concepts.aliases: casino problem, path dependence of ruin
concepts.source_title: The Logic of Risk Taking (Taleb, Incerto on Medium)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Casino example with one hundred persons vs one person a hundred days in a row on page.

concepts.name: Absorbing barrier
concepts.def: A state that, once hit, cannot be left: bankruptcy, a forced liquidation, a career end. With any fixed per-period ruin probability p, survival over n periods is (1 - p)^n and goes to zero, which is why Taleb says repetition makes paranoia about low-probability events rational. Expected-value reasoning that ignores the barrier is invalid.
concepts.formula: P(no ruin in n periods) = (1 - p)^n -> 0 as n -> inf for any p > 0
concepts.source_title: The Logic of Risk Taking (Taleb, Incerto on Medium)
concepts.originator: Probability theory of absorbing states; applied by Taleb, 2017
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Repetition and paranoia line on page; (1 - p)^n -> 0 for p > 0 is correct.

concepts.name: Uncle point
concepts.def: The loss level at which an investor is forced out of a strategy, by margin, mandate or nerve. Taleb argues no one gets the market's return without infinite pockets and no uncle points, so a model that assumes holding through any drawdown overstates achievable return.
concepts.aliases: cry uncle point, forced exit level
concepts.source_title: The Logic of Risk Taking (Taleb, Incerto on Medium)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Uncle point and infinite pockets lines on page.

concepts.name: Ruin precludes cost-benefit
concepts.def: Taleb's rule that where ruin is possible, cost-benefit analysis is no longer valid, because averaging a finite benefit against an absorbing loss has no meaning on a single path. It justifies hard constraints, such as the engine's expected-shortfall budget, above any expected-return optimization.
concepts.source_title: The Logic of Risk Taking (Taleb, Incerto on Medium)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page: if there is a possibility of ruin, cost benefit analyses are no longer possible.

concepts.name: Non-naive precautionary principle
concepts.def: A precautionary rule limited to fat-tailed, systemic ruin problems, where a system is at risk of total failure, rather than applied to every risk. It replaces risk estimates with a fragility-based approach and separates thin from fat tails and local from systemic harm, avoiding both paranoia and paralysis.
concepts.source_title: The Precautionary Principle (with Application to the Genetic Modification of Organisms) (arXiv 1410.5787)
concepts.originator: Taleb, Read, Douady, Norman and Bar-Yam, 2014
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract supports ruin-only scope, fragility approach and avoiding paralysis.

concepts.name: Local versus systemic harm
concepts.def: The distinction between harms that stay contained and can be averaged over (local, often thin-tailed) and harms that can propagate to the whole system (systemic, fat-tailed). Only the second class warrants precaution; for a portfolio it marks the difference between one position failing and the whole book or counterparty network failing.
concepts.source_title: The Precautionary Principle (with Application to the Genetic Modification of Organisms) (arXiv 1410.5787)
concepts.originator: Taleb, Read, Douady, Norman and Bar-Yam, 2014
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract separates local from systemic risk; portfolio application is editorial.

concepts.name: Mediocristan
concepts.def: Taleb's name for domains where no single observation can change the aggregate much: exceptions occur but carry no large consequences, and the sample mean and standard deviation are reliable.
concepts.source_title: The Fourth Quadrant: A Map of the Limits of Statistics (Edge, Sep 14, 2008)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Edge page defines Mediocristan as exceptions without large consequences; Taleb coined it in The Black Swan (2007).

concepts.name: Extremistan
concepts.def: Taleb's name for domains where exceptions can be everything: one observation can dominate the sum, the mean is unstable and tails drive outcomes. Wealth, market returns and casualties live here, so averages from history understate the future.
concepts.source_title: The Fourth Quadrant: A Map of the Limits of Statistics (Edge, Sep 14, 2008)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Edge page: in Extremistan exceptions can be everything.

concepts.name: Fourth quadrant
concepts.def: The cell of Taleb's two-by-two map where complex decisions (impact matters, not just frequency) meet Extremistan, the Black Swan domain where statistical models fail. His remedies are redundancy over optimization, avoiding prediction of remote payoffs, and not basing decisions on statistically based claims about tails.
concepts.aliases: limits of statistics map, four quadrants
concepts.source_title: The Fourth Quadrant: A Map of the Limits of Statistics (Edge, Sep 14, 2008)
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Page remedy is avoiding prediction of remote payoffs, and quadrants split by decision type, not exposure.

concepts.name: Grey swan
concepts.def: A large, consequential, low-frequency deviation that is still consistent with the known statistical properties of the process, unlike a Black Swan, which comes from incomplete knowledge.
concepts.source_title: Statistical Consequences of Fat Tails (Taleb, arXiv 2001.10488)
concepts.originator: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, 2007 (Mandelbrotian Gray Swan), formalized 2020
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Book defines Grey Swans as rare consequential deviations consistent with the known statistical properties.

concepts.name: Silent evidence
concepts.def: The evidence that never enters the record: after an event, explanation focuses on the signs that pointed to it while the many similar signs that led nowhere go unnoticed, so retrospective explanations look stronger than they are. In backtests it appears as dead strategies, delisted firms and untested rules, and it inflates apparent skill.
concepts.source_title: Review of The Black Swan by Richard Austin (IEEE Cipher, May 23, 2008)
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Review describes silent evidence as the many unnoticed signs that led nowhere, not failures in general.

concepts.name: Ludic fallacy
concepts.def: Taleb's term for basing studies of chance on the narrow world of games and dice, where the rules and probabilities are known. Real risk has unknown rules, so models calibrated as if markets were casinos miss model error itself.
concepts.source_title: Ludic fallacy (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Article: basing studies of chance on the narrow world of games and dice; The Black Swan 2007.

concepts.name: Fat Tony heuristic
concepts.def: When data contradict a model's premise, doubt the premise first. Asked for the odds of tails after 99 heads from a supposedly fair coin, Dr. John says 50:50 while Fat Tony says the coin is loaded. For an engine it means a run of extreme residuals is evidence against the model, not bad luck within it.
concepts.aliases: fat tonyism, the coin gotta be loaded, street-smart skepticism
concepts.source_title: Ludic fallacy (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Article: 99 heads, Dr. John says 50:50, Fat Tony says the coin gotta be loaded.

concepts.name: Via negativa
concepts.def: Taleb's adaptation of a theological method: improve outcomes by removing harmful things rather than adding interventions. Applied to a portfolio, cutting fragile exposures and leverage is more reliable than adding predictive signals.
concepts.source_title: Antifragile (book) (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Article: theological description by negation, broadened by Taleb to what to avoid.

concepts.name: Green lumber fallacy
concepts.def: Mistaking the visible, articulable knowledge for the knowledge that actually produces results; named after a trader who made money in green lumber without knowing what it was. It warns that a strategy's stated rationale may not be the source of its returns.
concepts.source_title: Antifragile (book) (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Article: mistaking one kind of knowledge for another; trader thought it was lumber painted green.

concepts.name: Optionality (Taleb)
concepts.def: The property of an exposure with limited downside and open upside, so that one needs to be right rarely, not often. Taleb's example is Thales renting olive presses cheaply before the harvest, which wins from positioning rather than forecasting.
concepts.source_title: Antifragile (book) (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Article covers Thales' olive-press option that did not depend on forecasting.

concepts.name: Intellectual Yet Idiot
concepts.def: Taleb's label for the semi-erudite expert who gets first-order logic right but misses second-order effects and cannot tell science from scientism. For a decision engine it is a warning against confident theory that ignores feedbacks and has no skin in the game.
concepts.source_title: The Intellectual Yet Idiot (Taleb, Incerto on Medium)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page: semi-erudite, first-order right but not second-order, cannot tell science from scientism, skin in the game.

concepts.name: Minority rule
concepts.def: An intransigent minority of about three or four percent can impose its preference on a flexible majority when the cost of complying is low, as with kosher drinks. Taleb analyzes it with renormalization across levels. In markets it explains why a small committed group of forced sellers or buyers can set prices.
concepts.aliases: dictatorship of the small minority, intransigent minority
concepts.source_title: The Most Intolerant Wins: The Dictatorship of the Small Minority (Taleb, Incerto on Medium)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page (Aug 14, 2016): three or four percent, kosher lemonade example, renormalization group.

concepts.name: Inverse problem of rare events
concepts.def: Inferring the generating process from data is hardest exactly where it matters: the rarer the event, the fewer observations constrain its probability and the larger the relative error. Taleb shows with 40 years of data that past Black Swans do not predict future ones.
concepts.aliases: the rarer the event the worse its inverse problem
concepts.source_title: The Fourth Quadrant: A Map of the Limits of Statistics (Edge, Sep 14, 2008)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page: the rarer the event the worse its inverse problem, samples must grow in inverse proportion to frequency; 40 years claim on page.

concepts.name: Kurtosis instability
concepts.def: The finding that sample kurtosis of market series is dominated by one observation: Taleb reports that 70 to 90% of the kurtosis in oil, the S&P 500, silver, UK rates, the Nikkei and US deposit rates over 40 years comes from a single day. Any tail statistic from history is therefore one day away from changing.
concepts.source_title: The Fourth Quadrant: A Map of the Limits of Statistics (Edge, Sep 14, 2008)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 70-90% from one day over 40 years for these series on page (list is longer).

concepts.name: Bleed versus blowup
concepts.def: Taleb's contrast between strategies that bleed small steady losses for rare large gains (long tails) and those that earn small steady gains until a blowup (short tails). He argues investors prefer the blowup profile because it looks good in short samples; AQR's response holds that selling catastrophe insurance earns positive long-run returns with sharp losses in bad times.
concepts.aliases: taleb distribution, picking up nickels in front of a steamroller
concepts.source_title: Do Financial Markets Reward Buying or Selling Insurance and Lottery Tickets? Author Response (AQR)
concepts.originator: Nassim Nicholas Taleb (Bleed or Blowup, Journal of Behavioral Finance)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: AQR cites Taleb's Bleed or Blowup and his claim investors dislike gradual bleeding more than blowups.

concepts.name: Bonus-blowup asymmetry
concepts.def: The agency problem where managers collect yearly bonuses on hidden tail risk and keep them after the blowup. Taleb's testimony states that bonuses do not accommodate the hidden risks of blow-ups. It predicts more short-tail strategies whenever incentives are annual and losses are rare.
concepts.aliases: bob rubin trade, heads i win tails you lose
concepts.source_title: Report on The Risks of Financial Modeling, VaR and the Economic Breakdown (Taleb, House Science Committee)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Bonuses line verbatim in the testimony.

concepts.name: Taleb's critique of VaR
concepts.def: Taleb's argument that Value at Risk gives false precision about rare events, is very sensitive to model specification at two standard deviations and beyond, and encourages untrained people to take risk with other people's money. His point that a model shows some risks but not the risks of using it applies to any single risk number.
concepts.source_title: Against Value-at-Risk: Nassim Taleb replies to Philippe Jorion (fooledbyrandomness.com)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Misplaced concreteness, 2 SD sensitivity, untrained people and model-risk lines on page.

concepts.name: Heuristic option pricing
concepts.def: Haug and Taleb's claim that traders price options with heuristics descended from Bachelier and Thorp and from put-call parity, which allow non-Gaussian distributions, rather than with the Black-Scholes-Merton formula. Implied volatility surfaces are thus a quoting device for fat tails, not evidence for the Gaussian model.
concepts.source_title: Option traders use (very) sophisticated heuristics, never the Black-Scholes-Merton formula (Haug and Taleb, JEBO 2011)
concepts.originator: Espen Gaarder Haug and Nassim Nicholas Taleb, 2011
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract supports the heuristic pricing claim; the implied-vol sentence is an inference, not a page claim.

concepts.name: Dynamic Hedging (Taleb)
concepts.def: Taleb's 1997 practitioner reference on hedging vanilla and exotic option books, built on the idea that the key to trading derivatives lies in implementing preventive risk management techniques, with a methodology for monitoring and managing portfolio risks.
concepts.source_title: Dynamic Hedging: Managing Vanilla and Exotic Options (Wiley, 1997)
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Page has the preventive risk management phrase (Jan 1997) but nothing on Greeks or higher-order sensitivities.

concepts.name: Cost-effective risk mitigation
concepts.def: Spitznagel's test for any hedge: it is worth holding only if the whole portfolio's expected compound growth rate rises net of the hedge's cost. Most diversifiers lower volatility and also lower compounding; an explosive crash payoff held in a small allocation can raise it. The engine should rank long Treasuries against this test, not against volatility reduction.
concepts.formula: Hedge is cost-effective if E[log(1 + r_p,hedged)] > E[log(1 + r_p,unhedged)]
concepts.source_title: Safe Haven: Investing for Financial Storms (Spitznagel, Wiley, Aug 10, 2021)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Taleb foreword: risk mitigation must raise your wealth; compound-growth formula is a correct formalization (Thorp blurb uses compound growth).

concepts.name: Risk-mitigation irony
concepts.def: Spitznagel's observation that conventional risk mitigation such as diversification smooths the ride but makes the investor poorer at the end of the day, whereas good risk mitigation should raise returns. Universa's analysis cited in Institutional Investor found a 60/40 mix trailed all stocks by 1% per year over 12 years.
concepts.aliases: the cost of safety, hedging drag
concepts.source_title: Nassim Taleb and Universa Versus the World (Institutional Investor, Sep 22, 2020)
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Page has no irony claim or cost-exceeds-risk claim; Spitznagel says diversification smooths the ride but makes you poorer.

concepts.name: Point forecasts under fat tails
concepts.def: Taleb, Bar-Yam and Cirillo argue that forecasting single values of fat-tailed variables violates probability theory, because the law of large numbers works too slowly or not at all. A Pareto 80/20 needs about 10^14 observations to match the significance of 30 Gaussian ones. Engines should forecast distributions and tail properties, not point outcomes.
concepts.source_title: On single point forecasts for fat tailed variables (Taleb, International Institute of Forecasters blog)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Post links the Taleb, Bar-Yam, Cirillo paper and gives the 10^14 figure.

concepts.name: Forecast martingale constraint
concepts.def: A probability forecast of a binary event must be a martingale and can be priced as a binary option. When uncertainty is high the fair value is pulled toward 50% and should move little even when polls swing, so a volatile forecast is an arbitrageable forecast.
concepts.aliases: election predictions as martingales, binary option forecast
concepts.source_title: Election Predictions as Martingales: An Arbitrage Approach (Taleb, arXiv 1703.06351)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract: binary option pricing, value near 50% under high uncertainty, small moves despite polls.

concepts.name: Quantile contribution bias
concepts.def: Sample estimates of the share held by the top centile are downward biased, unstable and rise with sample size under power-law tails. Apparent increases in concentration can be an artifact of more data rather than structural change, which matters for any index-concentration signal.
concepts.aliases: super-additivity of top shares, concentration estimator bias
concepts.source_title: On the Super-Additivity and Estimation Biases of Quantile Contributions (Taleb and Douady, arXiv 1405.1791)
concepts.originator: Nassim Nicholas Taleb and Raphael Douady, 2014
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract: downward biased, unstable, rise with population size, illusion of structural change.

concepts.name: Gini bias under infinite variance
concepts.def: When data have finite mean but infinite variance (tail index between 1 and 2), the nonparametric Gini coefficient is biased downward and the bias grows as the tail fattens; maximum likelihood fitting of the tail does better. It is another case where plug-in sample statistics understate fat-tailed reality.
concepts.source_title: Gini estimation under infinite variance (Fontanari, Taleb, Cirillo, arXiv 1707.01370)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract: tail index 1 to 2, downward bias growing as alpha falls, MLE better.

concepts.name: Minimum-variance numeraire
concepts.def: Taleb's requirement that a true currency be of minimum variance against an arbitrary basket of goods and services. He argues bitcoin fails this test and is neither a short nor long term store of value nor a safe haven.
concepts.aliases: numeraire test, store of value test
concepts.source_title: Bitcoin, Currencies, and Fragility (Taleb, arXiv 2106.14204)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract states the minimum-variance numeraire and the store-of-value and safe-haven claims.

concepts.name: Redundancy over optimization
concepts.def: Taleb's prescription for the fourth quadrant: hold slack, spare capacity and duplicate safeguards instead of optimizing, because a simple model error can blow through an optimized balance sheet; redundancy works like a long option. He adds that if you are leveraged, errors blow you up.
concepts.source_title: The Fourth Quadrant: A Map of the Limits of Statistics (Edge, Sep 14, 2008)
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Page has no sizing or model-optimal exposure claim; it says redundancy is like a long option and leverage turns errors into blowups.

concepts.name: Absence of volatility is not absence of risk
concepts.def: Taleb's warning that a quiet period says little about tail exposure, because fat-tailed risk can accumulate while realized volatility is low. It is the testable opposite of volatility targeting's premise and links to Minsky's view that stability breeds instability.
concepts.source_title: The Fourth Quadrant: A Map of the Limits of Statistics (Edge, Sep 14, 2008)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Warning is verbatim on page; volatility-targeting and Minsky links are editorial additions, not page claims.

concepts.name: Prevailing trend (Soros)
concepts.def: In Soros's account of boom-bust processes, the prevailing trend is the observable price or credit trend that participants' biased expectations reinforce and that is sustained by inertia once recognized. It is the 'reality' half of a reflexive pair whose other half is the prevailing bias. For a decision engine it marks the regime in which momentum is fed by belief rather than fundamentals alone.
concepts.source_title: George Soros, Fallibility, Reflexivity, and the Human Uncertainty Principle (Journal of Economic Methodology)
concepts.originator: George Soros, The Alchemy of Finance, 1987
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page describes an underlying trend that prevails in reality paired with a misconception, reinforced by expectations; originator fits (Alchemy 1987 named on page).

concepts.name: Cognitive and manipulative functions
concepts.def: Soros's two functions of a thinking market participant: the cognitive function tries to understand the world, and the manipulative function tries to change it to advance the participant's interests. When both operate at once they can interfere with each other, which is the root of reflexivity. The idea explains why market prices are not passive forecasts but inputs to the fundamentals they forecast.
concepts.aliases: participating function, cognitive function, manipulative function
concepts.source_title: George Soros, Fallibility, Reflexivity, and the Human Uncertainty Principle
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page names the cognitive and manipulative functions as described.

concepts.name: Human uncertainty principle
concepts.def: Soros's name for fallibility and reflexivity taken together: because participants' views are imperfect and those views change the situation they describe, outcomes in social systems carry uncertainty that cannot be removed by better data. It is a reason to treat model forecasts of markets as conjectures with irreducible error rather than as estimates converging on a fixed truth.
concepts.source_title: George Soros, Fallibility, Reflexivity, and the Human Uncertainty Principle
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page: 'I lump together the two concepts as the human uncertainty principle'.

concepts.name: Far-from-equilibrium conditions
concepts.def: Soros's term for market states in which positive feedback dominates, so that prices and fundamentals move away from each other and the normal, self-correcting rules of thumb stop working. Near equilibrium, negative feedback pulls views and reality together. A risk engine should expect estimated relations, such as stock-bond correlation or mean reversion, to break in far-from-equilibrium regimes.
concepts.source_title: George Soros, Fallibility, Reflexivity, and the Human Uncertainty Principle
concepts.originator: George Soros, The Alchemy of Finance, 1987
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page contrasts far-from-equilibrium and near-equilibrium, positive and negative feedback, and says normal rules do not apply.

concepts.name: Boom-bust asymmetry
concepts.def: Soros's observation that booms develop slowly and take a long time to become unsustainable, while busts tend to be abrupt. The shape implies negatively skewed returns late in a boom: small steady gains followed by a fast collapse. For sizing it argues that late-boom exposure should be judged by its tail, not its recent volatility.
concepts.aliases: slow boom fast bust, asymmetric boom-bust
concepts.source_title: George Soros, Fallibility, Reflexivity, and the Human Uncertainty Principle
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page: booms slow to develop, busts more abrupt.

concepts.name: Moment of truth
concepts.def: The point in Soros's boom-bust sequence when reality can no longer sustain the exaggerated expectations built up during the boom. It usually follows a period in which the gap between expectations and reality has widened. It is the turning signal that a regime model would most like to detect and the hardest to time.
concepts.source_title: George Soros, Fallibility, Reflexivity, and the Human Uncertainty Principle
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Moment of truth stage presented in the page's boom-bust sequence.

concepts.name: Twilight period
concepts.def: The stage after the moment of truth in Soros's sequence, when people keep playing the game though they no longer believe in it; it ends at the crossover point, where the trend turns down and prices lose their last prop, followed by a downward acceleration. Prices can still rise in this phase, so trend signals stay positive while conviction has gone. It is a regime in which trend and valuation signals disagree.
concepts.source_title: George Soros, Fallibility, Reflexivity, and the Human Uncertainty Principle
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page: twilight period when people continue to play the game though they no longer believe; crossover point follows.

concepts.name: Collateral-credit reflexive loop
concepts.def: Soros's simplest reflexive case: a real estate boom rests on the misconception that the value of collateral is independent of the availability of credit, when in fact easier credit raises collateral values, which supports more credit. The loop reverses when credit tightens. It links lending conditions to asset prices in both directions and is a core mechanism behind leverage cycles.
concepts.source_title: George Soros, Fallibility, Reflexivity, and the Human Uncertainty Principle
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page: misconception that the value of collateral is independent of the availability of credit.

concepts.name: Super-bubble (Soros)
concepts.def: Soros's thesis that repeated interventions by authorities to rescue markets from smaller busts allowed a decades-long credit expansion, a super-bubble that burst in 2007 to 2008. Each rescue reinforced the belief that markets correct themselves and encouraged more leverage. It frames policy support as a source of long-horizon fragility rather than only short-horizon safety.
concepts.source_title: George Soros, Fallibility, Reflexivity, and the Human Uncertainty Principle
concepts.originator: George Soros, The New Paradigm for Financial Markets, 2008
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page: interventions played a crucial role in a super-bubble that burst in 2007-2008; 2008 book in references.

concepts.name: Trading as conjecture and refutation
concepts.def: Soros's method of treating each position as a falsifiable hypothesis: formulate a conjecture, expose it to refutation, take a loss when proven wrong, and add to the bet when the market rather than the thesis appears wrong. It joins a Popperian research loop to position sizing. In an engine it maps to explicit invalidation conditions and to sizing that responds to evidence.
concepts.source_title: George Soros, Fallibility, Reflexivity, and the Human Uncertainty Principle
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page: formulate conjectures, expose them to refutation, take a loss when wrong, increase bet if market wrong; Popper linked.

concepts.name: Liquidity over earnings
concepts.def: Druckenmiller's principle that central bank policy and the movement of liquidity, not corporate earnings, drive the overall stock market. Earnings matter for single stocks, but index direction follows money and credit conditions. For a regime model it argues for rate and liquidity features ahead of earnings features at the market level.
concepts.aliases: liquidity moves markets, it's the fed
concepts.source_title: Livewire, Stanley Druckenmiller: The two things my mentor taught me (Apr 14, 2015)
concepts.originator: Stanley Druckenmiller, crediting his first mentor
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Livewire: earnings don't move the overall market, it's the Fed; focus on central banks and liquidity.

concepts.name: Eighteen-month horizon
concepts.def: Druckenmiller's rule to never invest in the present but to visualize the situation about 18 months ahead and position for that. Markets discount the future, so current conditions are already in the price. It suggests that forecast features should target changes over the next year or so rather than levels today.
concepts.aliases: never invest in the present, 18 months out
concepts.source_title: Livewire, Stanley Druckenmiller: The two things my mentor taught me (Apr 14, 2015)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Livewire: never invest in the present, visualize the situation 18 months from now.

concepts.name: Tudor Jones 200-day rule
concepts.def: Paul Tudor Jones's defensive rule to get out of anything that trades below its 200-day moving average of closing prices, which he described as his metric for everything he looks at. It is a binary regime filter that cuts exposure in downtrends at the cost of whipsaws. On monthly data the natural analog is price below its 10-month average.
concepts.formula: in_market = 1 if P_t > MA200_t else 0; monthly analog: trend_gap = P_t / MA10m_t - 1 > 0
concepts.source_title: 25iq, A Dozen Things I've Learned from Paul Tudor Jones (Jul 25, 2015)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 25iq: 200-day moving average as his metric and exit rule; formula is a correct indicator definition.

concepts.name: Five-to-one reward to risk
concepts.def: Tudor Jones's entry standard of risking one dollar to make five. At 5:1 a trader breaks even while right only about one time in six, so the rule lets a low hit rate coexist with positive expectancy. It is a constraint on trade selection, not a forecast, and assumes the stop is honored.
concepts.formula: breakeven win rate = 1 / (1 + R), with R = 5 giving 1/6
concepts.source_title: 25iq, A Dozen Things I've Learned from Paul Tudor Jones (Jul 25, 2015)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 25iq: risking one dollar to make five; breakeven p = 1/(1+R) = 1/6 at R = 5 is correct.

concepts.name: Performance-scaled trade size
concepts.def: The rule, stated by Tudor Jones, to decrease trading size when trading poorly and increase it when trading well. It is an anti-martingale applied to the trader's own equity curve: losses shrink exposure before they compound. It caps drawdowns from a broken edge but can also cut size just before a recovery.
concepts.aliases: size down when losing, equity-curve sizing
concepts.source_title: Habrador, Paul Tudor Jones: Losers average losers (Aug 2011)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Habrador: decrease volume when trading poorly, increase when trading well.

concepts.name: Losers average losers
concepts.def: Tudor Jones's maxim, kept on his office wall, that adding to a losing position is what losing traders do. It forbids averaging down on trades and asks for adding only to winners. It is the trading counterpart of the value investor's opposite habit, so its value depends on whether the horizon is trend-driven or mean-reverting.
concepts.aliases: never average losers, don't average down
concepts.source_title: Habrador, Paul Tudor Jones: Losers average losers (Aug 2011)
concepts.originator: Paul Tudor Jones; earlier Jesse Livermore
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Habrador: 'Losers Average Losers' picture on the wall (page says wall, not office specifically); minor.

concepts.name: Turtle N
concepts.def: The volatility unit of the Turtle system: N is the 20-day exponential moving average of the true range, started from a 20-day simple average. Every entry, stop and add-on is measured in N, which makes rules comparable across markets with very different prices. It is the original practical form of volatility-normalized trading.
concepts.formula: TR = max(H - L, H - C_prev, C_prev - L); N_t = (19 * N_{t-1} + TR_t) / 20
concepts.source_title: Hackernoon, Huobi Quant Academy (3): Turtle trading rules, citing Curtis Faith's Original Turtle Trading Rules
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Hackernoon: 20-day EMA of true range started from a 20-day simple average; TR and (19N + TR)/20 recursion are the standard correct form.

concepts.name: Turtle unit
concepts.def: The Turtle position size: a unit is sized so that a one-N move equals 1% of account equity, using the market's dollar volatility. Positions in volatile markets are therefore small and in quiet markets large, giving each trade roughly equal risk. It is volatility-scaled position sizing at the single-trade level.
concepts.formula: Unit = (0.01 * Equity) / (N * DollarsPerPoint)
concepts.source_title: Hackernoon, Huobi Quant Academy (3): Turtle trading rules
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Hackernoon: each N represents 1% of account equity; formula correct.

concepts.name: 2N stop
concepts.def: The Turtle stop rule: the stop sits 2N below the entry for longs and 2N above for shorts, so no trade can risk more than 2% of equity. In common implementations all units share one stop, moved to 2N from the newest entry when a unit is added. It ties stop distance to volatility rather than to a price level.
concepts.formula: stop_long = entry - 2N; risk per unit = 2N * DollarsPerPoint * Unit = 2% of equity
concepts.source_title: Hackernoon, Huobi Quant Academy (3): Turtle trading rules
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Page supports 2N stops, 2% cap and stops raised so all sit about 2N from newest unit; formula omits dollars per point, so risk is not in equity units.

concepts.name: Turtle unit limits
concepts.def: Caps on how many Turtle units can be held: 4 in a single market, 6 across closely correlated markets, 10 across loosely correlated markets and 12 in a single direction. They are a crude correlation-aware exposure budget layered on top of per-trade sizing. Without them, many signals in one theme would add up to one oversized bet.
concepts.source_title: Hackernoon, Huobi Quant Academy (3): Turtle trading rules
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Hackernoon lists 4, 6, 10 and 12 unit limits.

concepts.name: Turtle last-trade filter
concepts.def: The System 1 rule that a 20-day breakout signal is skipped if the previous System 1 breakout in the same direction was a winner; only losing breakouts reset the permission to trade, and System 2 has no skip rule. The article describes it as a filter to avoid entering trends that have already run. It shows how a conditioning rule on a signal's own recent record can change a system's trade count and drawdown.
concepts.source_title: MQL5, Automating Classic Market Methods (Part 5): The Original Turtle Trading Rules
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: MQL5 article supports the rule but says the skip applies to a winning prior breakout in the same direction and describes it as avoiding trends that have already run, not clustered false breakouts.

concepts.name: Turtle System 1 and System 2
concepts.def: The two Turtle entry systems: System 1 enters on a 20-day breakout and exits on a 10-day opposite breakout; System 2 enters on a 55-day breakout and exits on a 20-day opposite breakout, with no skip rule. Running both mixes a faster and a slower trend horizon. Both are Donchian channel breakouts, so the results depend on the markets' trendiness more than on fine tuning.
concepts.source_title: Hackernoon, Huobi Quant Academy (3): Turtle trading rules
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Hackernoon: System 1 20-day breakout, 10-day exit; System 2 55-day breakout, 20-day exit; skip rule stated only for System 1.

concepts.name: Portfolio heat
concepts.def: Seykota's term for the total risk carried across all open positions and bets in a portfolio, as opposed to the risk on any one trade. Heat is what the drawdown experience depends on, so it is the quantity a risk budget should cap. It maps directly to an aggregate expected-shortfall limit in a model book.
concepts.formula: heat = sum over open positions of (amount at risk to stop) / equity
concepts.source_title: Ed Seykota, Risk Management (2003 and 2015)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Seykota page defines portfolio heat as total risk across positions; formula is a fair sum-of-risk form.

concepts.name: Fixed fractional sizing
concepts.def: Betting a constant fraction of current equity on each trade rather than a constant amount. Seykota shows that the fixed-fraction system grows exponentially and overtakes a fixed-bet system, which grows linearly, and that betting too large a fraction leads to ruin. Kelly sizing is the growth-optimal special case.
concepts.formula: bet_t = f * W_t; W_T = W_0 * product(1 + f * x_t)
concepts.aliases: fixed fraction, percent risk sizing, fixed-fraction betting
concepts.source_title: Ed Seykota, Risk Management (2003 and 2015)
concepts.originator: Ed Seykota; earlier J. L. Kelly 1956
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Seykota: fixed fraction grows exponentially and surpasses linear fixed bet; Kelly section present; wealth product formula correct.

concepts.name: Continuous Kelly fraction
concepts.def: Thorp's continuous approximation of the Kelly bet for a security with expected return m, standard deviation s and riskless rate r: invest the fraction (m - r)/s^2 of capital, which gives the maximum growth rate r + (m - r)^2/(2 s^2). It is the bridge from betting to portfolio leverage, and it often implies leverage far above what parameter uncertainty can justify.
concepts.source_title: Edward O. Thorp, The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting, and the Stock Market (2006 Handbook version)
concepts.originator: Edward O. Thorp, 1997 to 2006; after Kelly 1956
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Thorp eq. 7.3: f* = (m - r)/s^2 and g = (m - r)^2/(2s^2) + r; correct.

concepts.name: Multi-asset Kelly
concepts.def: The portfolio form of Kelly: with covariance matrix C and excess-return vector M - R, the growth-optimal fractions are C^-1 (M - R). It requires C to be invertible, which fails when assets move in lockstep, and it is very sensitive to errors in expected returns. It explains why naive Kelly portfolios concentrate and lever up.
concepts.source_title: Edward O. Thorp, The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting, and the Stock Market (2006 Handbook version)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Thorp eq. 8.2: F* = C^-1[M - R], g = r + F*'CF*/2; correct.

concepts.name: Kelly growth ratio
concepts.def: Thorp's result that, with r = 0, betting c times the Kelly fraction yields c(2 - c) of the maximum growth rate. Half Kelly keeps 3/4 of the growth, and at twice Kelly the growth rate falls to zero, with negative growth beyond. It quantifies why overbetting is far costlier than underbetting.
concepts.formula: g(c f*) / g(f*) = c (2 - c), for r = 0
concepts.source_title: Edward O. Thorp, The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting, and the Stock Market (2006 Handbook version)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Thorp: c(2 - c) of maximum growth for 0 < c < 2; derivation checks with r = 0.

concepts.name: Kelly drawdown probability
concepts.def: Under Thorp's continuous model, the chance that wealth ever falls to a fraction x of its starting value when betting c times Kelly is x^(2/c - 1). At full Kelly the chance of ever losing half is 1/2; at half Kelly it is 1/8. It turns a sizing choice into a drawdown probability a risk budget can read.
concepts.source_title: Edward O. Thorp, The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting, and the Stock Market (2006 Handbook version)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Thorp: x^(2/c - 1); 1/2 at Kelly and 1/8 at half Kelly for x = 1/2; correct.

concepts.name: Stop-based position sizing
concepts.def: Kovner's method of setting the stop first, on a technical basis, and then sizing the position so that being stopped out costs a preset amount of equity. Size follows from the distance to the point where the trade is proven wrong. It makes risk per trade constant regardless of how wide the stop must be.
concepts.formula: size = (risk_fraction * equity) / |entry - stop|
concepts.source_title: Antoine Buteau, Lessons from Bruce Kovner
concepts.originator: Bruce Kovner, in Jack Schwager's Market Wizards, 1989
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Buteau: position size determined by the stop, stop set on a technical basis; formula correct.

concepts.name: Correlated positions as one bet
concepts.def: Kovner's warning that eight highly correlated positions are one position eight times as large. Diversification counts only to the extent positions are independent, so risk must be budgeted per theme, not per line. For an AI-buildout book of highly correlated megacaps, it implies the book is closer to one bet than nine.
concepts.formula: for n equal positions with volatility s and pairwise correlation rho: portfolio sd = s * sqrt(n + n(n - 1) rho)
concepts.aliases: correlated exposure aggregation, one big bet
concepts.source_title: Antoine Buteau, Lessons from Bruce Kovner
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Buteau quote verbatim; sd = s*sqrt(n + n(n-1)rho) for n unit positions is correct.

concepts.name: Triple confirmation (Marcus)
concepts.def: Michael Marcus's view that the best trades have fundamentals, technicals and market tone all pointing the same way. Each leg filters a different failure mode: a good story in a falling market, or a chart with no reason behind it. In an engine it corresponds to requiring agreement across independent signal families before sizing up.
concepts.source_title: The Investor's Podcast, Book review of Market Wizards
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Investor's Podcast: fundamentals, technicals and market tone, Marcus.

concepts.name: Profit-taking fallacy
concepts.def: Eckhardt's critique of the adage that you cannot go broke taking profits: cutting winners early while holding losers produces exactly the small-gain, large-loss profile that ruins traders. A trend-following edge comes from a few large winners, so truncating them removes the edge. It is the trading face of the disposition effect.
concepts.aliases: you can't go broke taking profits (critique)
concepts.source_title: NexusFi forum thread quoting William Eckhardt (The New Market Wizards)
concepts.originator: William Eckhardt, in The New Market Wizards, 1992
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NexusFi: Eckhardt calls the adage wrongheaded; professionals go broke taking small profits.

concepts.name: No model override
concepts.def: Simons's rule at Renaissance that the firm does what the model says regardless of how smart or dumb the trade looks at the moment. Discretionary overrides reintroduce the biases the model was built to remove and make results impossible to attribute. It requires that the model itself carry risk controls, since nobody will step in.
concepts.source_title: Alpha Architect, Secret Sauce: Jim Simons on Life and Building a Business (Nov 22, 2013)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Alpha Architect: slavishly use the models, do whatever it says; MIT 2010.

concepts.name: Main movement (Livermore)
concepts.def: Livermore's lesson that the big money is not in the individual fluctuations but in the main movements, and that it comes from sitting tight once right. Being right and sitting tight together is rare. It argues for trend exposure measured over months, with small swings ignored.
concepts.source_title: Edwin Lefevre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923), Project Gutenberg
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Gutenberg text: big money not in the individual fluctuations but in the main movements; sitting tight.

concepts.name: Livermore pivotal point
concepts.def: Livermore's entry levels: prior major tops and bottoms where price reversed, and round psychological levels such as 50, 100 or 200; he bought a breakout above one and sold a breakdown below one. A pivotal point is where the line of least resistance becomes clear. It differs from floor-trader pivot points, which are computed from the prior day's range.
concepts.source_title: Kitco, Jesse Livermore, world's greatest trader (May 2, 2023)
concepts.originator: Jesse Livermore, How to Trade in Stocks, 1940
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Kitco describes pivotal points as prior major tops and bottoms and round numbers like 50, 100, 200, buying breakouts and selling breakdowns.

concepts.name: Probe and add
concepts.def: Livermore's rule that it is foolhardy to make a second trade if the first trade shows a loss, since his speculative profits came from commitments showing a profit right from the start. Size is added only after the market confirms the first commitment. It is pyramiding with an explicit test step.
concepts.aliases: test positions, scale in on confirmation
concepts.source_title: Kitco, Jesse Livermore, world's greatest trader (May 2, 2023)
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Kitco has 'It is foolhardy to make a second trade, if your first trade shows you a loss' and profits from commitments showing a profit from the start, but no small test position wording.

concepts.name: Ten percent loss rule
concepts.def: Livermore's money-management rule never to sustain a loss of more than 10% of capital and to set a stop before making a trade. It is a hard cap on single-trade loss rather than a volatility-scaled one. On an index it translates to exiting after a 10% decline, which is a loose and likely whipsaw-prone analog.
concepts.formula: exit if loss_on_trade > 0.10 * capital
concepts.source_title: Kitco, Jesse Livermore, world's greatest trader (May 2, 2023)
concepts.originator: Jesse Livermore, How to Trade in Stocks, 1940
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Kitco: never sustain a loss of more than 10% of capital; always established a stop before a trade. Kitco cites the Smitten edition, not a dated 1940 text.

concepts.name: Templeton bull market life cycle
concepts.def: Templeton's four-stage sentiment cycle: bull markets are born on pessimism, grow on skepticism, mature on optimism and die on euphoria. It pairs with his rule that maximum pessimism is the best time to buy and maximum optimism the best time to sell. It maps sentiment and valuation states to expected forward returns.
concepts.aliases: bull markets are born on pessimism
concepts.source_title: Lauren Templeton, presentation at Ivey Business School (2012)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 2012 Templeton deck has both maxims attributed to Sir John Templeton.

concepts.name: Sleeping point
concepts.def: Baruch's sizing rule that the wisest course is to sell to the point where one stops worrying. It sizes a position by the owner's ability to hold it through stress rather than by a model alone. A position the holder will abandon at the bottom has a worse real payoff than its model payoff.
concepts.aliases: sell to the sleeping point, sell until you stop worrying
concepts.source_title: 25iq, A Dozen Things I've Learned from Bernard Baruch about Investing (May 7, 2016)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 25iq: sell to the point where one stops worrying; the label sleeping point is not on the page but the concept is.

concepts.name: Best long, worst short
concepts.def: Julian Robertson's description of Tiger's edge as a steady commitment to buying the best stocks and shorting the worst. The short book funds and hedges the long book, so returns depend on stock selection spread more than on market direction. It works poorly when markets reward momentum over price and earnings.
concepts.source_title: A Letter a Day, Letter #78: Julian Robertson (2000)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Letter: steady commitment to buying the best stocks and shorting the worst.

concepts.name: Exit when the market stops making sense
concepts.def: Robertson's March 2000 decision to stop subjecting investors to risk in a market he did not understand, where earnings and price took a back seat to mouse clicks and momentum. When the model of how prices are set stops working, the rule is to cut exposure rather than force the model. It is a regime-break exit, not a forecast that prices will fall.
concepts.aliases: robertson exit, step aside in irrational markets
concepts.source_title: A Letter a Day, Letter #78: Julian Robertson (2000)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Letter: no point subjecting investors to risk in a market he does not understand; mouse clicks and momentum.

concepts.name: Decade-low bottom
concepts.def: Jim Rogers's claim that bottoms in the investment world do not end with four-year lows but with 10- or 15-year lows. Real capitulation takes prices or valuations back to levels not seen in a decade or more. A testable form is a very low valuation percentile or a deep real drawdown.
concepts.source_title: Moomoo Learn, Jim Rogers: Invest only in what you have knowledge about
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Moomoo: bottoms don't end with four-year lows, they end with 10- or 15-year lows.

concepts.name: Move to breakeven
concepts.def: Peter Brandt's practice of moving a trade to a breakeven proposition as quickly as possible, raising the stop to entry once the trade has moved in his favor. It cuts the expected loss on trades that start well and fail, at the cost of more scratch trades. It fits a style where most trades lose and a few large winners pay for them.
concepts.source_title: Peter Brandt, Factor Trading blog, risk management posts (2016 to 2017)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Brandt Q&A post (Sep 22, 2016): move a trade to a breakeven proposition as quickly as possible; stop-to-entry is the mechanical equivalent.

concepts.name: Credibility theory
concepts.def: Credibility theory is the actuarial method for blending a risk's own experience with the experience of a wider class, weighting each by how predictive it is. It gives the best linear approximation to the Bayesian predictive mean. For a monthly equity-sizing engine it is the formal rule for how much a short live record of a strategy, regime or forecaster should move the engine away from its prior.
concepts.formula: estimate = Z * own_experience + (1 - Z) * class_experience, 0 <= Z <= 1
concepts.source_title: Credibility theory (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Wikipedia: credibility blends own and outside experience and seeks 'the best linear approximation to the mean of the Bayesian predictive density'; Whitney 1918 and Buhlmann named; formula is standard.

concepts.name: Limited fluctuation credibility
concepts.def: Limited fluctuation credibility grants full weight to own experience only when the data are large enough that the estimate lies within a relative error k of its true value with probability P; below that, weight grows with the square root of the data. The common standard of 1,082 claims corresponds to P = 90% and k = 5%. An engine can use it as a plain evidence gate: a strategy needs a stated number of independent observations before its own record replaces the prior, and partial credit before that.
concepts.formula: n0 = (y/k)^2 with Phi(y) = (1+P)/2; Z = min(1, sqrt(n/n0)); P = 0.90, k = 0.05 gives n0 = 1,082
concepts.aliases: classical credibility, full credibility standard, american credibility
concepts.source_title: Mahler and Dean, Credibility, Foundations of Casualty Actuarial Science ch. 8 (SOA STAM-22-18)
concepts.originator: Casualty actuaries from the CAS founding (Mowbray); tables in Longley-Cook, 1962 and Perryman, 1932
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Mahler and Dean give n0 = (y/k)^2, Phi(y) = (1+P)/2, 1,082 claims and the square root rule; Perryman 1932 and Longley-Cook 1962 are cited, Mowbray is not named on the page.

concepts.name: Square root rule for partial credibility
concepts.def: The square root rule sets partial credibility equal to the square root of the ratio of the data in hand to the full-credibility standard, capped at one. It follows from asking that the weighted estimate fluctuate no more than a fully credible one. For the engine it gives a simple schedule for phasing in a new signal: a quarter of the required months earns half weight.
concepts.formula: Z = min(1, sqrt(n / n_full))
concepts.source_title: Mahler and Dean, Credibility (SOA STAM-22-18), eq. 2.6.3
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Eq 2.6.3 is 'the important square root rule for partial credibility', Z = sqrt(n/n0), capped at 1; quarter-of-data gives half weight is correct.

concepts.name: Buhlmann credibility
concepts.def: Buhlmann credibility is the least squares linear estimator of a risk's mean, with weight Z = n/(n+K) on its own average and K the ratio of within-risk noise (EPV) to between-risk spread (VHM). Its estimates are the best linear least squares fits to Bayesian estimates, so it is Bayesian shrinkage without needing the full prior. An engine can apply it to any per-unit edge estimate (a forecaster, a regime's mean return, a strategy's Sharpe) by estimating EPV and VHM across the units and shrinking each toward the pooled mean.
concepts.formula: P = Z * Xbar + (1 - Z) * mu; Z = n / (n + K); K = EPV / VHM
concepts.aliases: greatest accuracy credibility, least squares credibility, bayesian credibility, buhlmann model
concepts.source_title: Dean, Topics in Credibility Theory (SOA STAM-23-18)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Dean gives Z = n/(n+K), K = EPV/VHM and calls it a linear least squares estimator; the best-linear-fit-to-Bayes sentence is not on Dean's note but is true and on the Wikipedia credibility page.

concepts.name: Expected value of the process variance
concepts.def: The expected process variance (EPV) is the average, across risks, of each risk's own random variance around its true mean. It is the noise term in Buhlmann credibility: the larger it is, the more data a risk needs before its own average deserves weight. For an equity engine, monthly return variance is very large relative to differences in true means, which is why EPV dominates and credibility of short records is low.
concepts.formula: EPV = E[ Var(X | Theta) ]
concepts.source_title: Dean, Topics in Credibility Theory (SOA STAM-23-18)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Dean defines EPV as the average process variance over risks, E[sigma^2(Theta)].

concepts.name: Variance of the hypothetical means
concepts.def: The variance of the hypothetical means (VHM) measures how much the true means of different risks differ from one another. It is the signal term in Buhlmann credibility; if it is zero, no risk's own experience carries information beyond the class mean. For an engine comparing strategies or regimes, a VHM estimate near zero is evidence that apparent differences in their records are noise.
concepts.formula: VHM = Var( E[X | Theta] )
concepts.aliases: vhm, between-group variance, variance of hypothetical means
concepts.source_title: Dean, Topics in Credibility Theory (SOA STAM-23-18)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Dean defines VHM as Var of hypothetical means mu(Theta).

concepts.name: Nonparametric credibility estimation
concepts.def: Nonparametric (empirical Bayes) credibility estimates EPV from the scatter within each risk and VHM from the scatter of risk means less the part explained by EPV. The VHM estimate can come out negative, in which case it is set to zero and every risk gets the class mean. An engine can run this each month on its stable of strategies or forecasters to get data-driven shrinkage weights instead of hand-set ones.
concepts.formula: EPV_hat = (1/r) * sum_i (1/(n-1)) * sum_j (X_ij - Xbar_i)^2; VHM_hat = (1/(r-1)) * sum_i (Xbar_i - Xbar)^2 - EPV_hat / n, floored at 0
concepts.aliases: empirical bayes credibility, nonparametric buhlmann estimation
concepts.source_title: Dean, Topics in Credibility Theory (SOA STAM-23-18)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Dean sec 2.1: EPV_hat with divisor R(N-1), VHM_hat = variance of risk means minus EPV_hat/N, zero when negative; called empirical Bayes.

concepts.name: Buhlmann-Straub credibility
concepts.def: The Buhlmann-Straub model extends Buhlmann credibility to observations of unequal size or exposure, replacing the count of observations n with total exposure m. Each observation's variance falls with its exposure, so large-exposure periods count for more. An engine can use it when evidence units differ in weight, such as regime spells of different length or forecasts scored over different numbers of months.
concepts.formula: Z_i = m_i / (m_i + K); Xbar_i = sum_j m_ij X_ij / m_i; K = EPV / VHM with Var(X_ij | Theta) = sigma^2(Theta) / m_ij
concepts.source_title: buhlmannStraub: Buhlmann-Straub credibility model (actuaRE)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: actuaRE page presents exposure-weighted Buhlmann-Straub with weighted means and credibility factors; stated formulas are the standard ones and correct.

concepts.name: Exact credibility
concepts.def: Exact credibility is the case where the linear credibility formula equals the full Bayesian posterior mean, which Jewell showed holds for all simple exponential families with natural conjugate priors. In that case nothing is lost by using the simple Z-weighted average. For the engine it justifies credibility weighting of normal-like quantities (mean returns, log vol) as fully Bayesian, and warns that heavy-tailed quantities fall outside the guarantee.
concepts.formula: E[mu(Theta) | X_1..X_n] = Z * Xbar + (1 - Z) * E[mu(Theta)] for exponential family likelihood with conjugate prior
concepts.source_title: Jewell, Credible Means are exact Bayesian for Exponential Families, ASTIN Bulletin 8(1), 1974
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Jewell abstract: credibility exact for simple exponential families and natural conjugate priors; formula correct.

concepts.name: Credibility and James-Stein equivalence
concepts.def: Buhlmann credibility and the James-Stein estimator are the same idea from two fields: both shrink each unit's average toward the grand mean by a factor set by noise over total variance, and both estimate that factor from the data. Efron and Morris showed the gain in practice, with Stein's rule 3.50 times as efficient as raw averages for baseball batting averages. For the engine it means a credibility weight is not a fudge: shrinking toward the estimated grand mean beats raw track records in total squared error once there are four or more units (three or more when shrinking toward a fixed prior).
concepts.formula: James-Stein: theta_i = Xbar + (1 - (k-3) * sigma^2 / V) * (X_i - Xbar), V = sum (X_i - Xbar)^2; Buhlmann: theta_i = Xbar + Z * (X_i - Xbar), Z = n / (n + EPV/VHM)
concepts.aliases: credibility as shrinkage, stein shrinkage in insurance
concepts.source_title: Efron and Morris, Data Analysis Using Stein's Estimator and Its Generalizations, JASA 70(350), 1975
concepts.originator: Efron and Morris, 1975, building on James and Stein
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Page supports 3.50 efficiency and shrinkage toward the grand mean with (k-3); with the grand mean estimated, Stein's rule dominates only with four or more units, not three. Page frames it as empirical Bayes and never says credibility.

concepts.name: Experience rating
concepts.def: Experience rating sets a policyholder's price partly from its own past losses rather than only from its class, with the blend set by credibility. Buhlmann framed it as dropping the assumption that risks in a class are identical. For the engine it is the principle that a market's own recent history (vol12, corr36) carries predictive weight for the next period, and the question is how much.
concepts.source_title: Buhlmann, Experience Rating and Credibility, ASTIN Bulletin 4(3), 1967
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Buhlmann 1967 abstract frames experience rating as dropping the homogeneity assumption.

concepts.name: Complement of credibility
concepts.def: The complement of credibility is the outside estimate that receives the weight 1 - Z, such as an industry rate or a prior expected loss ratio. Its choice matters as much as Z: a biased complement leaks bias into every estimate. In the engine the complement is the long-run prior (for example the 156-year unconditional equity premium or crash rate) that a regime's own short history is shrunk toward.
concepts.formula: weight on complement = 1 - Z
concepts.aliases: credibility complement, collective estimate, manual rate
concepts.source_title: Credibility theory (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Wikipedia presents weights Z and 1-Z on own and outside experience; the term 'complement of credibility' itself is not on the page.

concepts.name: Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem
concepts.def: The Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem says that for a wide class of distributions, the distribution of excesses over a high threshold converges to a generalized Pareto distribution as the threshold rises. It is the tail counterpart of the central limit theorem and the reason peaks over threshold works without knowing the parent distribution. For the engine it licenses fitting only the worst months (say beyond the 90th or 95th loss percentile) with a two-parameter GPD to estimate crash and shortfall risk.
concepts.formula: F_u(x) = P(X - u <= x | X > u); lim_{u -> x_F} sup_{0 <= x < x_F - u} | F_u(x) - G_{xi, beta(u)}(x) | = 0; G_{xi,beta}(x) = 1 - (1 + xi * x / beta)^(-1/xi)
concepts.aliases: second theorem of extreme value theory, pbdh theorem
concepts.source_title: Pickands-Balkema-De Haan theorem (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Wikipedia states excesses over a high threshold converge to a GPD and cites Balkema-de Haan 1974 and Pickands 1975; formula is the standard statement; the CLT comparison is the agent's gloss.

concepts.name: GPD shape parameter
concepts.def: The shape parameter xi of the generalized Pareto distribution sets how heavy the tail is: xi > 0 is a power-law tail, xi = 0 is exponential, xi < 0 has a finite end point. Moments of order 1/xi and higher are infinite, so xi near 0.5 implies infinite variance. For the engine, xi estimated on monthly losses is the single number that says how far beyond the 95th percentile a bad month can go, and its stability across eras is a direct test of tail model risk.
concepts.formula: xi = 1 / alpha where alpha is the tail index; E[X^r] infinite for r >= 1/xi when xi > 0
concepts.aliases: xi, tail shape, extreme value index
concepts.source_title: McNeil, Extreme Value Theory for Risk Managers (1999)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: McNeil 1999: for xi > 0 E[X^k] infinite for k >= 1/xi, xi = 1/2 gives infinite variance; xi = 1/alpha is standard.

concepts.name: Mean excess function
concepts.def: The mean excess function gives the expected size of the overshoot above a threshold u, given that u is exceeded. For a generalized Pareto tail it is linear in u with slope xi/(1-xi), so an upward-sloping empirical plot signals a heavy tail and the point where it turns linear suggests a threshold. For the engine it answers the question a sizing rule cares about: once a month is already bad, how much worse does it get on average.
concepts.formula: e(u) = E[X - u | X > u]; for GPD with xi < 1: e(u) = (sigma + xi * u) / (1 - xi)
concepts.aliases: mean residual life function, mean excess plot, me plot
concepts.source_title: meplot: Mean Excess Plot (VGAM documentation)
concepts.originator: Davison and Smith, 1990 (as a GPD diagnostic)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: VGAM page gives e(u) = (sigma + xi u)/(1-xi), linear in u; slope xi/(1-xi) is correct.

concepts.name: Threshold selection in peaks over threshold
concepts.def: Threshold selection is the choice of the level above which data are treated as GPD tail observations, trading bias (too low a threshold) against variance (too few exceedances). McNeil and Frey found results robust as long as the number of tail points is above about 50. With 156 years of monthly data, a threshold at the 95th loss percentile still leaves about 5% of 156 x 12 months, roughly 90 exceedances, well above that floor.
concepts.aliases: pot threshold, choice of u, number of exceedances k
concepts.source_title: McNeil and Frey, Estimation of tail-related risk measures for heteroscedastic financial time series (2000)
concepts.originator: Davison and Smith, 1990; McNeil and Frey, 2000
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: McNeil and Frey: 'as long as k is greater than about 50 the method is robust'; 5% of 1,872 months is about 94.

concepts.name: GPD tail estimator
concepts.def: The GPD tail estimator combines the empirical exceedance rate N_u/n with a fitted GPD to give tail probabilities beyond the data. It is valid only above the threshold. For the engine it converts a fitted monthly-loss tail into the probability of any named loss, such as a 20% month, which the empirical record may contain only once or twice.
