concepts.formula: F_hat(x) = 1 - (N_u / n) * (1 + xi_hat * (x - u) / beta_hat)^(-1/xi_hat), for x > u
concepts.aliases: smith tail estimator, pot tail estimator
concepts.source_title: McNeil, Extreme Value Theory for Risk Managers (1999), eq. 5
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Matches McNeil 1999 eq. 5.

concepts.name: EVT value at risk and expected shortfall
concepts.def: Inverting the GPD tail estimator gives VaR at any level beyond the threshold, and the linear mean excess of the GPD gives expected shortfall in closed form. The ES formula requires xi < 1. For the engine this is the cleanest way to compute the 12% monthly ES budget from a tail model rather than from a normal assumption, which McNeil warns is likely to underestimate tail risk.
concepts.formula: VaR_q = u + (beta/xi) * [ ((n/N_u) * (1 - q))^(-xi) - 1 ]; ES_q = VaR_q / (1 - xi) + (beta - xi * u) / (1 - xi)
concepts.aliases: pot var, gpd expected shortfall, evt risk measures
concepts.source_title: McNeil, Extreme Value Theory for Risk Managers (1999), eqs. 6 and 10
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Match McNeil 1999 eqs. 6 and 10; ES requires xi < 1.

concepts.name: Conditional EVT (GARCH-EVT)
concepts.def: Conditional EVT first filters returns with a volatility model, then fits a GPD to the tail of the standardized residuals, so tail quantiles scale with today's volatility. McNeil and Frey found it beat both unconditional EVT and normal GARCH in backtests, with normal models giving very bad expected shortfall estimates. For a monthly engine the analog is to scale a GPD fitted on vol-standardized monthly losses by current vol12, so the ES budget tightens automatically when volatility rises.
concepts.formula: VaR_q,t = mu_{t+1} + sigma_{t+1} * z_q; ES_q,t = mu_{t+1} + sigma_{t+1} * E[Z | Z > z_q]; z_q from the GPD fit to standardized residuals
concepts.aliases: garch-evt, mcneil-frey method, filtered historical evt
concepts.source_title: McNeil and Frey, Estimation of tail-related risk measures for heteroscedastic financial time series (2000)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: McNeil and Frey give x_q^t = mu + sigma z_q and S_q^t = mu + sigma E[Z|Z>z_q], and the backtest and ES findings.

concepts.name: Return period
concepts.def: A return period is the reciprocal of the annual exceedance probability: a 100-year flood has a 1 in 100 chance of being equaled or exceeded in any year, not a 100-year cycle. Such events can occur in consecutive years. For the engine it gives plain language for tail budgets: a 12% monthly ES set at a given level can be restated as a loss expected once every N months, and clusters of such losses are not proof the model is wrong.
concepts.formula: T = 1 / p, where p is the per-period exceedance probability
concepts.aliases: recurrence interval, 1-in-n event, annual exceedance probability, aep
concepts.source_title: USGS, Floods and Recurrence Intervals
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: USGS: 1 in 100 chance of being equaled or exceeded in any year, not a 100-year cycle, can occur in consecutive years; T = 1/p is implied by its examples.

concepts.name: Return level
concepts.def: The m-observation return level is the loss exceeded on average once every m observations. Under a GPD tail above threshold u with exceedance rate zeta_u it has a closed form. For the engine it gives the 1-in-120-month or 1-in-600-month monthly loss for the book, which can be checked against the realized record and used to size the long-Treasury hedge.
concepts.formula: x_m = u + (sigma/xi) * [ (m * zeta_u)^xi - 1 ] for xi != 0; x_m = u + sigma * log(m * zeta_u) for xi = 0
concepts.aliases: n-year return level, m-observation return level
concepts.source_title: TU Delft MUDE, GPD: m Return Levels
concepts.originator: Extreme value practice; POT form in Coles, An Introduction to Statistical Modeling of Extreme Values
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: TU Delft page gives both return level forms; it does not cite Coles, though Coles is the standard source of this form.

concepts.name: 1-in-200-year solvency standard
concepts.def: Solvency II sets the Solvency Capital Requirement at the Value-at-Risk of basic own funds at a 99.5% confidence level over one year, a loss expected once in 200 years. It fixes a horizon and a confidence level jointly, which is what makes the standard comparable across firms. For the engine it is an outside benchmark: the book's one-year 99.5% loss under the current sizing can be computed and reported next to the monthly 12% ES budget.
concepts.formula: SCR = VaR_0.995 of the one-year change in basic own funds
concepts.source_title: Solvency II Directive 2009/138/EC, Article 101 (EIOPA rulebook)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Article 101(3): VaR of basic own funds at 99,5 % over a one-year period.

concepts.name: Inverse cubic law of returns
concepts.def: The inverse cubic law is the finding that the cumulative distribution of large stock price moves decays as a power law with exponent alpha approximately 3, outside the Levy-stable range. In GPD terms this is a shape xi near 1/3: variance exists but the fourth moment does not. For the engine it is a prior for the tail shape when fitting monthly losses, and a reason kurtosis-based statistics on its 156-year record are unstable.
concepts.formula: P(|r| > x) ~ x^(-alpha), alpha approximately 3
concepts.source_title: Gopikrishnan, Meyer, Amaral and Stanley, Inverse Cubic Law for the Probability Distribution of Stock Price Variations (1998)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: arXiv abstract: alpha approximately 3, outside the Levy regime; xi = 1/3 implies finite variance and infinite fourth moment, correct.

concepts.name: Cramer-Lundberg model
concepts.def: The Cramer-Lundberg model describes an insurer's surplus as initial capital plus premium income at a constant rate, minus claims that arrive as a compound Poisson process. Ruin is the first time surplus goes below zero. For the engine the analog is the book's equity: capital is u, the expected excess return is the premium, and drawdowns are claims, so ruin theory gives the probability of ever hitting a drawdown limit for a chosen leverage.
concepts.formula: U(t) = u + c*t - S(t), S(t) = sum_{i=1}^{N(t)} X_i, N(t) Poisson with rate lambda
concepts.aliases: classical risk model, compound poisson surplus process
concepts.source_title: Koucha and dos Reis, Approximations to Ultimate Ruin Probabilities with a Wiener Process Perturbation (2021)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Koucha and dos Reis give U(t) = u + ct - S(t) with Poisson N(t) and credit Lundberg 1903; Cramer is not named on the page.

concepts.name: Net profit condition
concepts.def: The net profit condition requires premium income per unit time to exceed expected claims, c > lambda * mu, written as a positive safety loading theta. Without it ruin is certain. For the engine it says a position needs a positive expected excess return after costs to justify any size at all, and the size of the margin sets how fast ruin probability falls with capital.
concepts.formula: c - lambda * mu > 0; theta = c / (lambda * mu) - 1 > 0
concepts.source_title: Koucha and dos Reis, Approximations to Ultimate Ruin Probabilities with a Wiener Process Perturbation (2021)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page gives c - mu lambda > 0 and c = (1+theta) mu lambda; formula correct.

concepts.name: Adjustment coefficient
concepts.def: The adjustment coefficient R is the positive root of the Lundberg equation that balances premium income against the moment generating function of claims. It exists only when claims have exponential moments, that is, light tails. For the engine an analog R can be solved from the monthly return distribution at each leverage, giving an exponential rate at which the probability of a given drawdown falls; heavy tails make it fail to exist, which is itself a warning.
concepts.formula: lambda * (M_X(R) - 1) = c * R, R > 0 (classical case); random-walk analog: E[exp(-R * w * r)] = 1
concepts.source_title: Koucha and dos Reis, Approximations to Ultimate Ruin Probabilities with a Wiener Process Perturbation (2021)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page gives lambda(M_X(r)-1) = cr (sigma = 0) and assumes the claim MGF exists; random-walk analog is correct.

concepts.name: Lundberg's inequality
concepts.def: Lundberg's inequality bounds the probability of ultimate ruin by exp(-R * u), so with light-tailed claims ruin probability falls exponentially in starting capital. The Cramer approximation says this bound is tight up to a constant. For the engine it gives an upper bound on the chance that a sized book ever breaches its drawdown limit, valid only when monthly losses are light tailed.
concepts.formula: psi(u) <= exp(-R * u), u >= 0; psi(u) ~ C * exp(-R * u) as u -> infinity
concepts.source_title: Koucha and dos Reis, Approximations to Ultimate Ruin Probabilities with a Wiener Process Perturbation (2021)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page gives Psi(u) <= exp(-Ru) and Psi(u) ~ k exp(-Ru); the engine gloss should read as falling a set amount below starting capital, not drawdown from peak.

concepts.name: Ruin under heavy-tailed claims
concepts.def: When claim sizes are subexponential, no adjustment coefficient exists and ruin probability decays only like the integrated tail of the claim distribution, divided by the safety loading. Ruin then typically comes from one huge claim rather than a run of moderate ones. For the engine it means extra capital buys far less safety than Lundberg suggests, and the dominant ruin path is a single crash month, which favors explicit tail hedges over thicker cushions.
concepts.formula: psi(u) ~ (1/theta) * B0_bar(u), B0(x) = (1/mu) * integral_0^x B_bar(y) dy
concepts.aliases: subexponential ruin, embrechts-veraverbeke asymptotic, single big jump
concepts.source_title: Asmussen and Binswanger, Simulation of Ruin Probabilities for Subexponential Claims, ASTIN Bulletin 27(2), 1997
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Asmussen and Binswanger: R does not exist, psi(u) ~ (1/theta) B0_bar(u) per Embrechts and Veraverbeke, and only the largest claim causes ruin.

concepts.name: Chain ladder method
concepts.def: The chain ladder projects each accident year's cumulative claims to ultimate using age-to-age development factors averaged over past years. Its implicit model is that the expected next value equals the current value times a factor, independent across years. For the engine it is the template for projecting a partially observed outcome (a 12-month return or earnings year in progress) from its development so far, and its weakness is that it trusts thin early data completely.
concepts.formula: E[C_{i,k+1} | C_i1..C_ik] = C_ik * f_k; f_k_hat = sum_i C_{i,k+1} / sum_i C_ik; C_i,ult = C_i,current * product of remaining f_k
concepts.aliases: cl, development method, link ratio method
concepts.source_title: Mack, Distribution-Free Calculation of the Standard Error of Chain Ladder Reserve Estimates, ASTIN Bulletin 23(2), 1993
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Mack 1993 gives the expected value assumption and f_k_hat as the C_ik-weighted mean of factors.

concepts.name: Loss development factor
concepts.def: A loss development factor is the ratio of claims at one age to claims at an earlier age, and the cumulative factor to ultimate is the product of the remaining ones; its reciprocal is the share reported so far. It measures how much of the eventual outcome is already known. For the engine the analog is the fraction of a forecast horizon already elapsed, which sets how much weight realized data should get relative to the prior forecast.
concepts.formula: LDF_k = C_{k+1} / C_k; CDF_k = product_{j>=k} LDF_j; percent reported = 1 / CDF_k
concepts.aliases: ldf, age-to-age factor, link ratio, cdf
concepts.source_title: Bornhuetter-Ferguson method (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: BF Wikipedia page says percent reported is the reciprocal of the loss development factor; formulas correct.

concepts.name: Bornhuetter-Ferguson method
concepts.def: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson method estimates ultimate losses as reported losses plus a prior expected loss times the percent still unreported. It ignores early noise in the unreported part and leans on the prior until the data mature, a blend of chain ladder and expected-loss methods. For the engine it is the right way to update a 12-month view mid-horizon: keep the realized part, and take the unrealized part from the prior forecast rather than extrapolating the first few months.
concepts.formula: Ultimate = Reported + U0 * (1 - 1/CDF); Reserve_BF = (1 - p_k) * U0 with p_k = 1/CDF
concepts.aliases: bf method, expected loss ratio blend
concepts.source_title: Bornhuetter-Ferguson method (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Wikipedia: reported plus a priori expected losses times percent unreported, 1972 paper, a blend of chain ladder and expected claims methods.

concepts.name: Benktander method
concepts.def: The Benktander method is a credibility mixture of chain ladder and Bornhuetter-Ferguson, giving the chain ladder weight c equal to the proportion of ultimate already paid. Mack found it almost always has a smaller mean squared error than either parent, except with extremely volatile or extremely stable patterns. For the engine it is a ready-made rule for blending a prior forecast with partial realized data, with weight on data rising as the horizon elapses.
concepts.formula: R_c = c * R_CL + (1 - c) * R_BF with c = p_k; equivalently R_GB = (1 - p_k) * U_BF
concepts.source_title: Mack, Credible Claims Reserves: The Benktander Method, ASTIN Bulletin 30(2), 2000
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Mack 2000: c = p_k, R_GB = q_k U_BF, smaller MSE unless the pattern is extremely volatile or stable; both formula forms are algebraically equal.

concepts.name: Mack chain ladder standard error
concepts.def: Mack's model states the variance assumption implicit in the chain ladder, that the variance of next-period claims is proportional to current claims, and derives a distribution-free standard error for reserve estimates. It splits error into process risk and parameter risk. For the engine the same split applies to any projected outcome: report both the noise of the future path and the estimation error of the factors used to project it.
concepts.formula: Var(C_{i,k+1} | C_i1..C_ik) = C_ik * sigma_k^2; mse(R_i) = process variance + estimation variance
concepts.aliases: mack model, mack 1993, distribution-free chain ladder
concepts.source_title: Mack, Distribution-Free Calculation of the Standard Error of Chain Ladder Reserve Estimates, ASTIN Bulletin 23(2), 1993
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Mack 1993: variance assumption and mse as process variance plus estimation error (page says estimation error, not parameter risk).

concepts.name: Claims development result
concepts.def: The claims development result is the change in the best estimate of ultimate claims between two successive valuation dates, the one-year view of reserve risk. Under the distribution-free chain ladder with known factors, its expected value is zero by the martingale property. For the engine the analog is the month-to-month revision of its own 12-month forecast: unbiased forecasts produce revisions with mean zero and no autocorrelation, which is a direct self-test.
concepts.formula: CDR_i(I+1) = E[C_iJ | D_I] - E[C_iJ | D_{I+1}]; E[CDR | D_I] = 0 (known factors)
concepts.source_title: Merz and Wuthrich, Modelling the Claims Development Result for Solvency Purposes, CAS E-Forum Fall 2008
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Merz and Wuthrich Definition 2.4 and expected CDR of zero for known CL factors.

concepts.name: Kaplan-Meier estimator
concepts.def: The Kaplan-Meier estimator gives a survival curve as the product, over event times, of one minus the share of those at risk who fail at that time. It handles right-censored cases that have not yet failed. For the engine it estimates how long regimes, bull markets or drawdowns last, counting the current unfinished spell correctly as censored instead of dropping it.
concepts.formula: S_hat(t) = product over t_i <= t of (1 - d_i / n_i)
concepts.source_title: Kaplan-Meier estimator (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Wikipedia: product-limit estimator for right-censored data; formula standard (math did not render in fetch).

concepts.name: Greenwood's formula
concepts.def: Greenwood's formula gives the approximate variance of a Kaplan-Meier survival estimate, growing as fewer cases remain at risk. It is derived by the delta method on the log survival estimate. For the engine it puts error bars on regime-duration curves, which matter because the long tails of those curves rest on a handful of spells.
concepts.formula: Var[S_hat(t)] approx S_hat(t)^2 * sum over t_i <= t of d_i / (n_i * (n_i - d_i))
concepts.source_title: Kaplan-Meier estimator (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Wikipedia names Greenwood's formula, derived via log survival and the delta method, citing Greenwood 1926; formula is the standard one.

concepts.name: Right censoring
concepts.def: A right-censored observation is one whose event has not occurred by the end of observation, so only a lower bound on its duration is known. Dropping such cases biases durations down; treating them as failures does the same. For the engine the live regime and the current drawdown are always right-censored, and so is any strategy still running.
concepts.source_title: Kaplan-Meier estimator (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Wikipedia defines right-censoring as no event by last follow-up.

concepts.name: Survival function
concepts.def: The survival function gives the probability that a lifetime exceeds t, and the hazard rate is the instantaneous failure rate among survivors; each determines the other. Actuarial mortality tables are tabulated survival functions. For the engine it is the frame for asking whether the chance a regime ends depends on its age, which decides whether a Markov model with constant transition rates is adequate.
concepts.formula: S(t) = P(T > t); h(t) = f(t) / S(t); S(t) = exp(- integral_0^t h(s) ds)
concepts.source_title: Kaplan-Meier estimator (Wikipedia)
concepts.originator: Life-table actuarial practice; Kaplan and Meier, 1958 (nonparametric estimate)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Wikipedia defines S(t) as probability life is longer than t and uses the hazard rewriting; formulas correct.

concepts.name: Gompertz law of mortality
concepts.def: Gompertz's law says the force of mortality rises geometrically with age, from the idea that a person loses equal portions of remaining power to resist death in equal intervals. It is the opposite of a Lindy pattern. For the engine it is the hypothesis that a bull regime or a trend becomes more fragile the longer it runs, testable with regime-duration hazards.
concepts.formula: mu_x = a * q^x (often written B * c^x), x = age
concepts.source_title: Gompertz, On the Nature of the Function Expressive of the Law of Human Mortality, Phil. Trans. 115 (1825)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Gompertz 1825, Phil. Trans. 115: equal portions of remaining power to oppose destruction, intensity a q^x.

concepts.name: Constant hazard of public firms
concepts.def: Daepp and coauthors found that more than 25,000 North American public companies from 1950 to 2009 died (by merger, buyout or liquidation) at an approximately constant hazard, independent of age and sector, with a typical half-life of about a decade. That is neither Lindy (falling hazard) nor Gompertz (rising hazard). For the engine it is a base rate for how long a single-name position stays a listed going concern, and a reminder that concentrated books carry a steady exit hazard.
concepts.formula: S(t) = exp(-lambda * t); half-life = ln(2) / lambda, about 10 years
concepts.source_title: Daepp, Hamilton, West and Bettencourt, The mortality of companies, J. R. Soc. Interface 12(106), 2015
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract supports 25,000+ firms, 1950-2009, constant hazard, half-life about a decade, any sector; the merger, buyout or liquidation detail is not in the abstract; half-life formula correct.

concepts.name: Lee-Carter model
concepts.def: The Lee-Carter model writes log mortality at each age and year as an age profile plus an age sensitivity times one common time index, which is forecast as a random walk with drift. It is a one-factor model fitted by singular value decomposition and remains the standard benchmark. For the engine it is a template for a one-factor model of a term structure of risk, such as crash probabilities across horizons or ES across names, driven by one market-wide index.
concepts.formula: ln(m_{x,t}) = a_x + b_x * k_t + e_{x,t}; sum_x b_x = 1; sum_t k_t = 0; k_t random walk with drift
concepts.source_title: Petnehazi and Gall, Mortality rate forecasting: can recurrent neural networks beat the Lee-Carter model? (2019)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Petnehazi and Gall give the equation, constraints, SVD fit, random walk with drift, and call it the leading statistical model; cite Lee and Carter 1992.

concepts.name: Excess-of-loss layer
concepts.def: An excess-of-loss layer pays the part of a loss above an attachment point, capped at a limit. By simple algebra its payoff is a call spread on the loss: long a call struck at the attachment, short one struck at attachment plus limit. For the engine it is the shape of a tail hedge sized to the ES budget, paying only for monthly losses between, say, 10% and 30%, and priced from the GPD tail.
concepts.formula: L = min(max(X - a, 0), l) = max(X - a, 0) - max(X - a - l, 0)
concepts.aliases: xl layer, excess of loss reinsurance, l xs a
concepts.source_title: Proteus Actuarial Library, Reinsurance Contracts (XoL.apply)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Proteus page: layer_loss = min(max(loss - excess, 0), limit); call-spread identity is correct math.

concepts.name: Catastrophe model
concepts.def: A catastrophe model has four modules: a hazard catalog of simulated events, an exposure module of what is at risk and policy terms, a vulnerability module of damage given intensity, and a financial module that applies terms and aggregates losses. The industry adopted them after Hurricane Andrew caused $20 billion in insured losses in 1992. For the engine the same split organizes stress testing: shock catalog, book weights, per-name sensitivity, and portfolio P&L after hedges.
concepts.source_title: NAIC, Catastrophe Models (Property)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NAIC page: four components, introduction in the 1980s, Hurricane Andrew $20 billion in 1992 spurred adoption.

concepts.name: Vulnerability function
concepts.def: A vulnerability function maps hazard intensity at a site to expected damage for a type of exposure. It is where nonlinearity lives: small shocks do little, large ones destroy. For the engine it is the per-holding response to a market shock, which for levered or high-beta names like TSLA is convex in the shock and should not be a single linear beta.
concepts.source_title: NAIC, Catastrophe Models (Property)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NAIC: the vulnerability module quantifies expected damage for the exposures from an event given local event strength.

concepts.name: Exceedance probability curve
concepts.def: An exceedance probability curve gives, for each loss level, the probability that losses in a year exceed it, on an occurrence (largest event) or aggregate basis. Average annual loss is the area under it. For the engine an EP curve of monthly or annual book losses is a fuller report than one VaR or ES number and shows directly how a hedge layer cuts the curve.
concepts.formula: EP(x) = P(L > x); AAL = E[L] = integral_0^inf EP(x) dx
concepts.aliases: ep curve, oep, aep curve, loss exceedance curve
concepts.source_title: NAIC, Catastrophe Models (Property)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NAIC describes EP curves on aggregate or occurrence basis and AAL; AAL as area under EP is correct for nonnegative losses.

concepts.name: Solvency Capital Requirement
concepts.def: The Solvency Capital Requirement is the capital a European insurer must hold, calibrated to the 99.5% one-year Value-at-Risk of basic own funds and computed by a standard formula or an approved internal model. It is a risk-sensitive capital rule rather than a fixed ratio. For the engine it is the model for tying position size to a capital measure: size so that the tail loss at a fixed confidence and horizon stays within capital.
concepts.formula: SCR = VaR_0.995 (one-year loss in basic own funds)
concepts.source_title: Solvency II Directive, Article 101 (EIOPA rulebook)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Article 101(3) calibration matches; standard formula or internal model is Article 100, not this page.

concepts.name: Own risk and solvency assessment
concepts.def: The own risk and solvency assessment (ORSA) requires an insurer to assess its overall solvency needs given its own risk profile and tolerance limits, its continuous compliance with capital rules, and how far its risk profile deviates from the assumptions behind the standard capital formula. It must be part of business strategy and inform decisions on an ongoing basis. For the engine it is a monthly self-assessment: state where the book's actual risk departs from the model's assumptions and act on it.
concepts.source_title: Solvency II Directive, Article 45 (EIOPA rulebook)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Article 45 elements (a)-(c) and the integral-part-of-strategy wording match.

concepts.name: Equity symmetric adjustment
concepts.def: Solvency II's symmetric adjustment raises the standard equity capital charge when an equity index is above its weighted average level and lowers it when below, within 10 percentage points either way. The delegated rules use a 36-month average. For the engine it is a regulator's countercyclical sizing rule that can be tested directly: tighten the equity risk budget after rallies and loosen it after falls.
concepts.formula: SA = 0.5 * ((CI - AI) / AI - 8%), bounded at -10% and +10% (AI = 36-month weighted average index level)
concepts.aliases: equity dampener, sa, symmetric adjustment mechanism
concepts.source_title: Solvency II Directive, Article 106 (EIOPA rulebook)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Article 106 supports index vs weighted average and the 10-point cap; the 36-month average and the 8% term are from Delegated Regulation 2015/35 Art 172, not this page, and are correct.

concepts.name: Actuarial standards of practice
concepts.def: Actuarial standards of practice (ASOPs) are the US professional standards that govern actuarial work by credentialed US actuaries. ASOP 25 on credibility procedures, effective May 1, 2014, defines credibility as the predictive value the actuary attaches to a set of data and asks the actuary to use an appropriate credibility procedure when blending subject experience with relevant experience. For the engine it is a ready checklist for its evidence gate.
concepts.aliases: asop, asop 25, asop 56, actuarial standards board
concepts.source_title: Actuarial Standards Board, ASOP No. 25 Credibility Procedures
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: ASOP 25 page supports the blending requirement but does not mention ASOP 56 (it cross-references ASOPs 35 and 41 only); def trimmed to what the page supports.

concepts.name: Actuarial work review
concepts.def: IFoA standard APS X2, in force since 1 July 2015, sets requirements for work review and independent peer review of actuarial work by members. The point is that a second qualified person checks reasoning and results before they are relied on. For the engine it supports a rule that a new sizing rule or model change is not live until an independent check (a second agent or a frozen out-of-sample test) has passed it.
concepts.aliases: aps x2, peer review, independent peer review
concepts.source_title: IFoA, Actuarial Profession Standard (APS) X2
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: IFoA page: APS X2 imposes requirements on Work Review and Independent Peer Review, in force 1 July 2015.

concepts.name: Process risk versus parameter risk
concepts.def: Actuaries split prediction error into process risk, the randomness of outcomes even with known parameters, and parameter risk, the error in the estimated parameters themselves. Mack's chain ladder standard error is built from both parts. For the engine the split matters because parameter risk does not diversify over time: a mis-estimated equity premium biases every month, so it should widen the ES estimate rather than average out.
concepts.formula: MSE = process variance + estimation variance
concepts.aliases: process variance and estimation error, parameter uncertainty
concepts.source_title: Mack, Distribution-Free Calculation of the Standard Error of Chain Ladder Reserve Estimates, ASTIN Bulletin 23(2), 1993
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Mack 1993 splits mse into stochastic error (process variance) and estimation error; formula correct.

concepts.name: Ensemble prediction system
concepts.def: A forecasting system that runs the same model many times from slightly perturbed initial states (and often perturbed model physics) so that the spread of the runs estimates forecast uncertainty. Its output is a sample from a predictive distribution rather than one trajectory. For a decision engine it is the template for producing a distribution of outcomes from many plausible starting states instead of a single point forecast.
concepts.aliases: eps, ensemble forecast, ensemble forecasting system
concepts.source_title: 25 years of ensemble forecasting at ECMWF (ECMWF Newsletter 153)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Newsletter 153 describes N perturbed forecasts covering initial and model uncertainty; ECMWF and NCEP first operational ensembles in 1992.

concepts.name: ECMWF ENS
concepts.def: The medium-range ensemble of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts: one control forecast plus 50 members with slightly altered initial conditions and model physics, at about 9 km resolution and out to 15 days. It is the benchmark against which new physical and machine-learning ensembles are scored. It shows that an operational forecaster can publish uncertainty every day as a routine product.
concepts.source_title: ECMWF: Medium-range forecasts
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 51 members, perturbed IC and physics, about 9 km, 15 days verified; Dec 19 1992 start is on Newsletter 153, not this page.

concepts.name: NOAA GEFS
concepts.def: The Global Ensemble Forecast System of the US National Centers for Environmental Prediction, with 31 members (30 perturbed plus 1 control), run four times a day at about 25 km resolution out to 16 days, and to 35 days for the 00 UTC cycle. It is the main US operational ensemble and the source of a long reforecast archive. Its existence beside ENS illustrates that independent ensembles can be combined into a multi-system forecast.
concepts.aliases: gefs, global ensemble forecast system, gefsv12
concepts.source_title: NOAA EMC: Global Ensemble Forecast System
concepts.originator: NCEP, first operational ensemble 1992; version 12 Sep 23, 2020
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 31 members, four runs, about 25 km, 16/35 days, operational since Dec 1992, v12 Sep 23 2020 all on page.

concepts.name: Ensemble mean filtering
concepts.def: Averaging the ensemble members acts as a nonlinear filter that removes the unpredictable scales on which members disagree and keeps the predictable signal; for fields such as precipitation the ensemble mean is about as skilful as the high-resolution forecast early on and more skilful thereafter. The mean is not a realistic scenario, only a good point estimate. For a market engine this is why an average of many forecasters beats the typical forecaster, and why the average should not be read as a path.
concepts.source_title: Palmer et al., Ensemble prediction: a pedagogical perspective (ECMWF Newsletter 106)
concepts.originator: Palmer, Buizza, Hagedorn, Lawrence, Leutbecher and Smith, 2006
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Page describes the nonlinear filtering effect, but says the mean beats the high-resolution forecast after early days for some fields, not that it beats any single member.

concepts.name: Flow-dependent predictability
concepts.def: Forecast uncertainty does not grow at a fixed rate: some initial states are highly predictable and others are not, and an ensemble can tell which is which while a single run cannot. The usefulness of an ensemble comes largely from this state dependence of its spread. For a market engine it means predictive variance should be conditional on the regime, not a constant.
concepts.source_title: Palmer et al., Ensemble prediction: a pedagogical perspective (ECMWF Newsletter 106)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page: some initial states highly predictable, others not, and the ensemble forecasts this flow-dependent predictability.

concepts.name: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions
concepts.def: In a chaotic deterministic system, nonperiodic solutions are unstable, so slightly differing initial states can evolve into very different states. Lorenz showed this in a simple convection model and used the result to examine the feasibility of very long range weather prediction. For a decision engine it sets a hard limit on point forecasts and is the reason to forecast distributions.
concepts.aliases: butterfly effect, lorenz chaos, chaos theory, deterministic chaos
concepts.source_title: Lorenz, Deterministic nonperiodic flow (Meteo-France library record)
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Instability of nonperiodic solutions verified, but the abstract only says feasibility of very-long-range prediction is examined, not concluded infeasible.

concepts.name: Lorenz 1963 system
concepts.def: A three-variable system of ordinary differential equations, reduced from a model of convection, whose solutions with the classic parameters wander on a strange attractor and never repeat. It is the standard toy model for chaos, data assimilation and ensemble tests. It is useful as a synthetic test bed where the true predictability of a forecaster is known.
concepts.formula: dx/dt = sigma (y - x); dy/dt = x (rho - z) - y; dz/dt = x y - beta z; classic sigma = 10, rho = 28, beta = 8/3
concepts.source_title: Lorenz system (Wikipedia)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Equations and sigma 10, rho 28, beta 8/3 match; convection model from 1963 with strange attractor.

concepts.name: Predictability horizon
concepts.def: The lead time beyond which a forecast cannot beat climatology because initial errors have grown to saturation. Weather science separates a practical limit (about 10 days for skillful deterministic midlatitude forecasts today) from an intrinsic limit (about two weeks) that would remain even with a near-perfect model. A market engine needs the same split: how far ahead its signals add skill, and how far any signal could.
concepts.aliases: predictability limit, intrinsic predictability, practical predictability, two-week limit
concepts.source_title: Zhang et al., What is the predictability limit of midlatitude weather? (J. Atmos. Sci. 2019)
concepts.originator: Lorenz 1969; quantified by Zhang et al., 2019
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Practical about 10 days and intrinsic about 2 weeks verified in Zhang et al. 2019.

concepts.name: Forecast skill horizon
concepts.def: The lead time at which an ensemble stops outperforming a climatological distribution, measured with a proper score such as the CRPS. Buizza and Leutbecher found it between 16 and 23 days for instantaneous grid-point fields and longer for time and space averages. The idea transfers directly: an engine should measure, by horizon, where its log score stops beating the unconditional distribution, and expect averaged targets (12-month returns) to keep skill longer than point targets.
concepts.formula: h* = smallest lead h at which mean score skill versus climatology is not positive
concepts.source_title: Buizza and Leutbecher, The forecast skill horizon (ECMWF Tech Memo 754)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Definition, CRPS, 16 to 23 days and longer for averaged fields verified; h* formula consistent.

concepts.name: Error doubling time
concepts.def: The time it takes a small forecast error to double under the system's own dynamics. Lorenz's 1969 analogue study gave a raw estimate of eight days and corrected values of 2.5 and 5 days, and he showed smaller scales double faster, which is why shrinking initial error buys little extra range. In markets the analog is how fast a valuation or macro signal's predictive edge decays with horizon.
concepts.formula: e(t) ~ e0 * 2^(t / T_d) in the small-error regime
concepts.source_title: Shen, Pielke, Zeng and Zeng, Exploring the origin of the two-week predictability limit (Atmosphere 2024)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Eight days raw, 2.5 and 5 corrected, smaller scales faster growth on page; exponential doubling formula correct.

concepts.name: Constructed analogue
concepts.def: A forecast built from a weighted linear combination of past observed states, with weights fit by ridge regression so the combination matches today's state, then applied to what followed each past state. Van den Dool introduced it because close natural analogues are very unlikely in high-dimensional systems with short records. It is the regularized cousin of nearest-neighbour analog forecasting for a market state vector.
concepts.formula: w = argmin ||x_now - sum_j w_j x_j||^2 + lambda ||w||^2; forecast = sum_j w_j y_(j+h)
concepts.source_title: NOAA CPC: Constructed Analogue (CA) prediction of SST (van den Dool)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Ridge-weighted combination of past states applied to what followed; natural analogues unlikely in high-dof processes; cites van den Dool 1994.

concepts.name: Data assimilation
concepts.def: The process of combining a model forecast (the background or first guess) with new observations, each weighted by its error covariance, to produce the best estimate of the current state. It is how weather centres start every forecast and a large part of why skill has improved. For a market engine it is the discipline of updating latent states such as expected return or regime with each month's data rather than refitting from scratch.
concepts.source_title: Data assimilation (Wikipedia)
concepts.originator: Operational NWP practice; Kalman 1960 for the linear theory
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Background/first guess corrected by observations weighted by estimated errors; Kalman filter linked; Kalman 1960 not cited on page.

concepts.name: Ensemble Kalman filter
concepts.def: A Kalman filter in which the forecast error covariance is estimated from an ensemble of model runs instead of being propagated with linearized equations. Evensen's Monte Carlo approach avoids the closure problem of the extended Kalman filter, where higher-order moments are dropped. It suits a nonlinear market engine that already simulates many paths and needs a covariance to weight new data.
concepts.formula: K = P_f H^T (H P_f H^T + R)^-1, with P_f the sample covariance of the forecast ensemble; each member x_a = x_f + K (y + eps - H x_f)
concepts.source_title: Evensen, Sequential data assimilation for nonlinear dynamics: the ensemble Kalman filter
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Ensemble-estimated covariance, no EKF closure problem, gain formula and perturbed observations on page; 1994 year not on this chapter.

concepts.name: 4D-Var
concepts.def: Four-dimensional variational assimilation finds the initial state that best fits a background estimate and all observations spread over a time window, subject to the model's own dynamics, by minimizing a cost function. ECMWF made it operational on Nov 25, 1997. The market analog is fitting a latent state path to a window of data under a dynamic model, penalized toward a prior.
concepts.formula: J(x0) = 1/2 (x0 - xb)^T B^-1 (x0 - xb) + 1/2 sum_i (y_i - H_i(x_i))^T R_i^-1 (y_i - H_i(x_i)), subject to x_(i+1) = M_i(x_i)
concepts.source_title: Bannister, Variational data assimilation: background and methods (Reading/ECMWF training)
concepts.originator: Operational at ECMWF Nov 25, 1997 (Rabier et al., 2000)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Cost function and model constraint match Bannister slides; Nov 25 1997 date is not on this page but confirmed by Rabier et al. 2000 (QJRMS 126).

concepts.name: Three types of forecast goodness
concepts.def: Murphy split forecast goodness into consistency (the forecast matches the forecaster's true judgment), quality (the forecast matches what happened) and value (the benefit a decision maker gets from using it). Quality and value are related nonlinearly and not always monotonically, so a better score does not guarantee better decisions. A risk engine should report all three: is the output its honest belief, does it score, and does acting on it pay.
concepts.source_title: Murphy, What is a good forecast? An essay on the nature of goodness in weather forecasting (Weather and Forecasting 1993)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Consistency, quality, value and nonlinear, non-monotonic quality-value relation verified.

concepts.name: Murphy decomposition of the Brier score
concepts.def: Murphy's 1973 partition of the Brier score into reliability (how far binned forecast probabilities sit from observed frequencies), minus resolution (how much the observed frequency varies across bins), plus uncertainty (the base-rate variance, outside the forecaster's control). It tells whether a binary forecast is losing points to miscalibration or to lack of discrimination. For a crash probability it separates a fixable calibration error from an absence of signal.
concepts.formula: BS = (1/N) sum_k n_k (p_k - obar_k)^2 - (1/N) sum_k n_k (obar_k - obar)^2 + obar (1 - obar)
concepts.aliases: brier decomposition, reliability resolution uncertainty, murphy decomposition
concepts.source_title: WWRP/WGNE Joint Working Group on Forecast Verification Research: Forecast verification methods
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Murphy 1973 partition and formula match the page.

concepts.name: Reliability term
concepts.def: The first term of the Brier decomposition: the count-weighted mean squared gap between each forecast probability bin and the frequency actually observed in that bin. Zero means perfect calibration of the binary forecast. It can be fixed after the fact by recalibration, unlike resolution.
concepts.formula: REL = (1/N) sum_k n_k (p_k - obar_k)^2
concepts.source_title: JWGFVR: Forecast verification methods
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: REL term matches page formula.

concepts.name: Forecast resolution
concepts.def: The ability of a forecast to sort outcomes into groups whose observed frequencies differ from the base rate; in the Brier decomposition it is the count-weighted variance of the observed frequency across forecast bins. A forecast that always issues the base rate is perfectly reliable but has zero resolution. Resolution is the part of skill that cannot be manufactured by recalibration, so it is the true test of whether a market signal knows anything.
concepts.formula: RES = (1/N) sum_k n_k (obar_k - obar)^2
concepts.source_title: JWGFVR: Forecast verification methods
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page defines resolution as sorting events into subsets and says a climatology forecast has no resolution; RES formula matches.

concepts.name: Brier uncertainty term
concepts.def: The third Brier term, obar(1 - obar), depends only on the observed base rate and is the Brier score of always forecasting that base rate. It is why raw Brier scores cannot be compared across events of different frequency. Crash probabilities in calm and turbulent samples must be compared by skill score, not raw score.
concepts.formula: UNC = obar (1 - obar)
concepts.source_title: JWGFVR: Forecast verification methods
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: UNC = ybar(1 - ybar) on page; equals Brier score of the constant base-rate forecast (correct math).

concepts.name: Skill score
concepts.def: A normalized score that expresses a forecast's accuracy as the fraction of the possible improvement over a reference forecast, usually climatology or persistence, that it achieves. It is 1 for a perfect forecast, 0 for no improvement and negative when the forecast is worse than the reference. It is the standard way to say whether a market model beats the no-skill baselines it must beat.
concepts.formula: SS = (S_forecast - S_reference) / (S_perfect - S_reference)
concepts.aliases: forecast skill, skill relative to climatology, reduction of variance
concepts.source_title: JWGFVR: Forecast verification methods
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Generic skill score formula and persistence/climatology references on page; upper bound 1, 0 no improvement.

concepts.name: Brier skill score
concepts.def: The Brier score of a forecast expressed relative to the Brier score of a reference, usually climatology. It is unstable in small samples and for rare events, which need many cases. Monthly crash12 forecasts with only a few dozen independent crashes since 1871 fall squarely into that warning.
concepts.formula: BSS = 1 - BS / BS_reference
concepts.source_title: JWGFVR: Forecast verification methods
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: BSS = 1 - BS/BS_ref and small-sample, rare-event instability warning on page.

concepts.name: Climatological reference forecast
concepts.def: The no-information forecast that issues the long-run distribution of the variable, ignoring current conditions; with persistence it is the usual baseline in skill scores. A forecast that cannot beat it has no skill however good it looks. For monthly stock returns the analog is the expanding-window unconditional distribution of real returns known at each date.
concepts.aliases: climatology, climatological forecast, unconditional forecast, reference forecast
concepts.source_title: JWGFVR: Forecast verification methods
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Climatology and persistence named as usual reference forecasts.

concepts.name: Rank histogram
concepts.def: A diagnostic that tallies where each observation falls among the sorted ensemble members; flat suggests the right spread, U-shaped too little spread, dome-shaped too much, and lopsided a bias. Hamill warned that a flat histogram can come from unreliable ensembles and that a U shape can reflect conditional bias. It is a sanity check on any engine that outputs simulated paths, not a proof of quality.
concepts.source_title: Hamill, Interpretation of rank histograms for verifying ensemble forecasts (2001)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Hamill 2001 abstract: flat can come from unreliable ensembles, U-shape can reflect conditional bias; Anderson and Talagrand not on page but correct history.

concepts.name: Probability integral transform
concepts.def: The value of the predictive CDF at the realized outcome, u_t = F_t(x_t). If forecasts are ideal and continuous, these values are independent uniform draws on (0,1). It turns any sequence of distributional forecasts, such as monthly mixture-of-normals return forecasts, into numbers that can be tested for calibration.
concepts.formula: u_t = F_t(x_t); for a normal mixture u_t = sum_k w_k Phi((x_t - mu_k) / sigma_k)
concepts.source_title: Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery, Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness (JRSS B 2007)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: PIT u_t = F_t(x_t), uniform for ideal continuous forecasts, Dawid 1984 credited; mixture CDF formula correct.

concepts.name: PIT histogram
concepts.def: A histogram of PIT values used as the continuous-forecast counterpart of the rank histogram: flat means probabilistically calibrated, U-shaped means the predictive distributions are too narrow, hump-shaped means too wide, and sloped means biased. Gneiting and Katzfuss name it as the practical calibration check. For a return engine it shows at a glance whether tails are hit too often.
concepts.source_title: Gneiting and Katzfuss, Probabilistic forecasting (Annual Review of Statistics 2014)
concepts.originator: Dawid 1984; Diebold et al. 1998; shape interpretation in Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery, 2007
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: SSRN abstract names PIT histograms as the calibration check and shapes are in the 2007 JRSS B paper, but that paper credits Dawid 1984 and Diebold et al. 1998 for PIT-based evaluation.

concepts.name: Continuous ranked probability score
concepts.def: A strictly proper score for a predictive CDF against a real-valued outcome, equal to the integrated squared gap between the forecast CDF and the step function at the outcome. It generalizes absolute error, is in the units of the variable and is less punishing of a miss in the tails than the log score. It is a robust second score for a return engine whose primary score is the log score.
concepts.formula: CRPS(F, y) = integral (F(x) - 1{y <= x})^2 dx = E|X - y| - 0.5 E|X - X'|, X and X' independent draws from F (loss orientation)
concepts.aliases: crps, ranked probability score for continuous variables, energy score in one dimension
concepts.source_title: Gneiting and Raftery, Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation (JASA 2007)
concepts.originator: Matheson and Winkler 1976; Hersbach 2000; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Integral and kernel forms match JASA (which uses positive orientation; loss form stated correctly); Matheson and Winkler 1976 and Hersbach 2000 cited.

concepts.name: CRPS of a normal forecast
concepts.def: The closed-form CRPS when the predictive distribution is normal, obtained by partial integration. It makes minimum-CRPS fitting of Gaussian post-processing models fast. It is the building block for scoring each component of a mixture-of-normals return forecast.
concepts.formula: CRPS(N(mu, sigma^2), y) = sigma [ z (2 Phi(z) - 1) + 2 phi(z) - 1/sqrt(pi) ], z = (y - mu) / sigma (loss orientation)
concepts.source_title: Gneiting and Raftery, Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation (JASA 2007)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Closed form sigma[z(2Phi(z) - 1) + 2phi(z) - 1/sqrt(pi)] is correct in loss orientation and is in JASA and Gneiting et al. 2005 Eq 5.

concepts.name: CRPS of a normal mixture
concepts.def: The closed form of the CRPS for a weighted mixture of normal distributions, written with the expected absolute value of a normal variable. It lets an engine that already outputs a Gaussian mixture compute the CRPS exactly each month without simulation. It also applies to BMA predictive distributions, which are mixtures.
concepts.formula: CRPS(sum_m w_m N(mu_m, s_m^2), y) = sum_m w_m A(y - mu_m, s_m^2) - 0.5 sum_m sum_n w_m w_n A(mu_m - mu_n, s_m^2 + s_n^2), with A(mu, s^2) = 2 s phi(mu/s) + mu (2 Phi(mu/s) - 1)
concepts.source_title: Grimit, Gneiting, Berrocal and Johnson, The continuous ranked probability score for circular variables (UW Tech Report 493, 2006)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Formula matches Grimit et al. Eq 5 and A(mu, s^2) in Eq 6; BMA use noted on page.

concepts.name: Logarithmic score
concepts.def: The log of the predictive density at the realized outcome; it is strictly proper and, by Bernardo's result, essentially the only proper local score. In base 2 and negated it is the ignorance score, which Roulston and Smith tie to the returns of betting in proportion to forecast probabilities. It is the engine's primary score, and differences in mean log score are directly log-wealth differences for a Kelly bettor.
concepts.formula: LogS(f, y) = log f(y); ignorance IGN = -log2 f(y)
concepts.aliases: log score, ignorance score, logarithmic scoring rule, log predictive density
concepts.source_title: Gneiting and Raftery, Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation (JASA 2007)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: LogS = log p, Bernardo 1979 local-score result on JASA page; ignorance -log2 f matches Roulston and Smith.

concepts.name: Interval score
concepts.def: A proper score for a central prediction interval that adds the interval width to a penalty, scaled by 2/alpha, for each unit by which the outcome falls outside. It rewards narrow intervals only if they cover. It is the natural score for the 12-month return range the engine publishes alongside its point forecast.
concepts.formula: S_alpha(l, u; x) = (u - l) + (2/alpha)(l - x) 1{x < l} + (2/alpha)(x - u) 1{x > u} (loss orientation)
concepts.source_title: Gneiting and Raftery, Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation (JASA 2007)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Formula matches JASA Eq 43 (negatively oriented); traced to Dunsmore 1968 and Winkler 1972.

concepts.name: Forecast sharpness
concepts.def: The concentration of the predictive distributions, a property of the forecasts alone; narrower intervals are sharper. Sharpness is only a virtue when calibration holds, because an overconfident forecaster is also sharp. It is measured for a return engine by the average predictive standard deviation or average central interval width.
concepts.source_title: Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery, Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness (JRSS B 2007)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Sharpness is concentration of predictive distributions and a property of the forecasts only.

concepts.name: Sharpness subject to calibration
concepts.def: The principle that probabilistic forecasting should maximize the sharpness of predictive distributions subject to calibration. It orders the checks: first confirm statistical consistency with outcomes, then prefer the most concentrated forecast. It is a model-selection rule an evidence gate can apply to competing return forecasters.
concepts.aliases: maximize sharpness subject to calibration, gneiting paradigm
concepts.source_title: Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery, Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness (JRSS B 2007)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract paradigm verbatim in JRSS B 2007.

concepts.name: Probabilistic calibration
concepts.def: A sequence of distributional forecasts is probabilistically calibrated if, on average over time, outcomes fall below each forecast p-quantile a fraction p of the time; this is essentially uniformity of the PIT. It is the formal version of saying a 10% tail should be hit 10% of the time. It is weaker than ideal forecasting and can hold for forecasts with no skill.
concepts.source_title: Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery, Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness (JRSS B 2007)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Essentially PIT uniformity; climatological forecaster example shows calibration without conditional skill.

concepts.name: Marginal calibration
concepts.def: A forecast sequence is marginally calibrated when the time-averaged forecast CDF equals the time-averaged distribution of outcomes, which the authors read as equality of observed and forecast climatology. A return engine can be probabilistically calibrated yet forecast too fat or too thin an unconditional distribution. Checking both catches different failures.
concepts.source_title: Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery, Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness (JRSS B 2007)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Equality of observed and forecast climatology stated in paper.

concepts.name: Spread-skill relationship
concepts.def: In a perfect ensemble the time-mean spread about the ensemble mean equals the time-mean RMS error of the ensemble mean, and days with larger spread should have larger errors. ECMWF reports the spread-error relation of its EPS is good, with slight under-dispersion for 850 hPa temperature. For a return engine it asks whether months with a wide predictive distribution are actually the months with large surprises.
concepts.formula: spread-skill ratio = sqrt(mean predictive variance) / RMSE of predictive mean; 1 for a calibrated system
concepts.source_title: Palmer et al., Ensemble prediction: a pedagogical perspective (ECMWF Newsletter 106)
concepts.originator: Operational ensemble verification; Palmer et al., 2006
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Perfect-EPS spread equals RMS error verified, but the page does not say real ensembles show a weak spread-error correlation; it calls the ECMWF relation good.

concepts.name: Ensemble underdispersion
concepts.def: The common failure in which ensemble members cluster too tightly, so observations fall outside the ensemble range too often and the rank histogram is U-shaped. Gneiting et al. found raw and bias-corrected temperature ensembles strikingly underdispersive, with a nominal 66.7% range covering 28.7% and 31.1% of outcomes. Models fit on calm samples tend to share this overconfidence.
concepts.aliases: underdispersion, overconfident ensemble, too little spread
concepts.source_title: Gneiting, Raftery, Westveld and Goldman, Calibrated probabilistic forecasting using EMOS and minimum CRPS estimation (MWR 2005)
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Strikingly underdispersive verified, but bias-corrected coverage was 31.1%, so not both under 30%.

concepts.name: Model output statistics
concepts.def: A post-processing method that regresses observed weather on the variables a numerical model forecasts, so the regression learns and removes the model's systematic biases. Glahn and Lowry introduced it as an objective forecasting technique, and NOAA still runs it with multiple linear regression and forward selection. For a market engine it is the step that maps raw model output to the realized outcome before anything is reported.
concepts.source_title: NOAA MDL: What is MOS?
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Glahn and Lowry 1972, statistical relationship to model output, corrects systematic biases, multiple linear regression with forward selection.

concepts.name: Ensemble model output statistics
concepts.def: A post-processing method that turns an ensemble into a Gaussian predictive distribution whose mean is a bias-corrected weighted average of the members and whose variance is a linear function of the ensemble variance. Coefficients are fit over a sliding training window by minimizing the mean CRPS. It is the simplest recalibration layer to put on top of a return engine's predictive mean and variance.
concepts.formula: y ~ N(a + b1 X1 + ... + bm Xm, c + d S^2), S^2 the ensemble variance
concepts.source_title: Gneiting, Raftery, Westveld and Goldman, Calibrated probabilistic forecasting using EMOS and minimum CRPS estimation (MWR 2005)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Gaussian with mean a + sum b_i X_i and variance c + dS^2 fit over sliding window by minimum CRPS.

concepts.name: Minimum CRPS estimation
concepts.def: Fitting the parameters of a predictive distribution by choosing the values that optimize the mean CRPS over the training data, rather than by maximum likelihood. Because CRPS is less sensitive to a few extreme cases, the fit is more robust in short windows. It is an alternative to maximum log score fitting when the training window is short or contaminated by a crash.
concepts.formula: theta_hat = argmin_theta (1/n) sum_t CRPS(F_theta,t, y_t)
concepts.aliases: minimum score estimation, optimum score estimation
concepts.source_title: Gneiting, Raftery, Westveld and Goldman, Calibrated probabilistic forecasting using EMOS and minimum CRPS estimation (MWR 2005)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Coefficient values that optimize the CRPS for training data; robustness stated relative to ignorance score and ML.

concepts.name: Ensemble Bayesian model averaging
concepts.def: A post-processing method in which the predictive density is a weighted mixture of kernels, one centred on each bias-corrected ensemble member, with weights equal to each member's posterior probability of being best over a training window, estimated by EM. Its variance splits into between-forecast spread and within-forecast error, which explains why ensembles can show spread-error correlation and still be underdispersive. It natively produces the mixture of normals that the engine already outputs.
concepts.formula: p(y | f_1..f_K) = sum_k w_k g_k(y | f_k), with y | f_k ~ N(a_k + b_k f_k, sigma^2); w_k and sigma by EM maximum likelihood
concepts.aliases: bma for ensembles, ensemble bma, ensemblebma
concepts.source_title: Raftery, Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Polakowski, Using Bayesian model averaging to calibrate forecast ensembles (MWR 2005)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Normal kernels around a_k + b_k f_k with common sigma, posterior-best weights, EM, and between/within variance decomposition explaining underdispersion verified.

concepts.name: Reforecast
concepts.def: A long archive of retrospective forecasts made with one frozen version of the current model over many past years, so that statistical post-processing has a large, consistent training sample. Hamill, Whitaker and Mullen found that calibration with a reforecast let an older, coarser model beat a newer high-resolution one for US precipitation. For a market engine it is the rule that the deployed model must be rerun walk-forward over the full history before its recalibration is fit.
concepts.source_title: Hamill, Whitaker and Mullen, Reforecasts: an important dataset for improving weather predictions (BAMS 2006)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Frozen 1998 GFS reforecast; calibrated older model beats 2002 higher-resolution GFS for US precipitation.

concepts.name: Cost-loss decision model
concepts.def: A two-action decision model in which a user can pay a cost C to protect against an adverse event or risk a loss L if it occurs unprotected. With reliable probability forecasts the optimal rule is to act whenever the event probability exceeds C/L, so users with different cost-loss ratios need different thresholds. It converts a crash probability into a de-risking rule.
concepts.formula: act if p > C/L; expected expense of acting = C, of not acting = p L
concepts.aliases: cost/loss model, cost-loss ratio, static cost-loss model
concepts.source_title: Richardson, Predictability and economic value (ECMWF)
concepts.originator: Classic decision model; applied to ensembles by Richardson, 2000
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Act when probability exceeds own cost-loss ratio; expense formulas correct.

concepts.name: Relative economic value
concepts.def: The fraction of the saving that a perfect forecast would give over acting on climatology alone that a real forecast achieves, for a user with a given cost-loss ratio. It is plotted against C/L because value varies by user, peaks for users whose C/L equals the event base rate, and the peak equals the Peirce skill score. Richardson showed ensemble probabilities give more value than a single control run for all users who pick their own threshold.
concepts.formula: V = (E_climate - E_forecast) / (E_climate - E_perfect); max V = H - F at C/L = obar
concepts.aliases: potential economic value, value score, pev
concepts.source_title: Richardson, Predictability and economic value (ECMWF)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: V definition, peak at climatological frequency equal to Peirce score, and probabilities beat control for all users verified.

concepts.name: Peirce skill score
concepts.def: The hit rate minus the false alarm rate of a yes/no forecast. It is unaffected by the base rate in the sense that random or constant forecasts score zero, and it equals the maximum relative economic value of the forecast. It is the natural single number for a crash-warning rule.
concepts.formula: PSS = H - F = hits/(hits + misses) - false alarms/(false alarms + correct negatives)
concepts.aliases: hanssen-kuipers discriminant, true skill statistic, kss, tss
concepts.source_title: Richardson, Predictability and economic value (ECMWF)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page names max value H - F the Peirce skill score (also Kuipers, true skill statistic); formula correct; Peirce 1884 is standard history.

concepts.name: Anomaly correlation coefficient
concepts.def: The correlation between forecast and observed departures from climatology, the headline skill measure of medium-range weather forecasting; ECMWF tracks the lead time at which 500 hPa height ACC falls to 60%. It ignores bias, so a high ACC does not guarantee accurate forecasts. Its market twin is the correlation of forecast and realized excess returns, which says nothing about calibration.
concepts.formula: AC = sum (f - c)(o - c) / sqrt( sum (f - c)^2 * sum (o - c)^2 ), c the climatological mean
concepts.source_title: JWGFVR: Forecast verification methods
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Formula matches page and page says AC is not sensitive to bias; 60% at 500 hPa threshold is from ECMWF node 25701, not this page.

concepts.name: Weather roulette
concepts.def: A verification game in which a forecaster bets each day against a casino that sets odds from a reference forecast (in Palmer et al., a Gaussian centred on the high-resolution deterministic forecast with spread from its past errors), staking in proportion to its forecast probabilities and reinvesting. Wealth grows by the forecaster's log score advantage over the casino's reference, so it translates log score skill into compounding money; with climatology as the reference it is the cleanest bridge from the engine's log score to its implied Kelly growth.
concepts.formula: log(W_T / W_0) = sum_t [ log f_t(y_t) - log c_t(y_t) ], f the forecast and c the casino's reference probability of the realized bin
concepts.source_title: Palmer et al., Ensemble prediction: a pedagogical perspective (ECMWF Newsletter 106)
concepts.originator: Leonard Smith and Mark Roulston (credited in Palmer et al., 2006); Roulston and Smith, 2002
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Palmer et al. set casino odds from a Gaussian around the high-resolution deterministic forecast, not climatology, and credit Smith and Roulston.

concepts.name: Quiet revolution of weather prediction
concepts.def: Bauer, Thorpe and Brunet's description of numerical weather prediction's progress as a steady accumulation of scientific knowledge and technological advances that, with few exceptions, were not physics breakthroughs. The review cites Simmons and Hollingsworth (2002) for a gain of about one day of lead time per decade; ECMWF separately reports a 60% anomaly correlation moving from about day 5 in the early 1980s to about day 8 by 2010. It is the base rate for how fast a well-run forecasting enterprise improves: slowly, through data, assimilation and verification discipline.
concepts.aliases: a day per decade, nwp progress, quiet revolution
concepts.source_title: Bauer, Thorpe and Brunet, The quiet revolution of numerical weather prediction (Nature 2015)
concepts.originator: Bauer, Thorpe and Brunet, 2015; Simmons and Hollingsworth, 2002
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Quiet revolution framing and one day per decade (via Simmons and Hollingsworth ref) verified on Nature page; the day 5 to day 8 figures come from ECMWF 2010, not this review.

concepts.name: Seasonal forecast reliability limits
concepts.def: Seasonal forecasts have real but patchy skill: Weisheimer and Palmer rated reliability from 5 (perfect) to 1 (dangerously useless) and found tropical temperature often useful while summer rainfall over Northern Europe was rated dangerous. Skill depends on region, season and variable, and on slow drivers such as ENSO. The market lesson is that long-horizon return forecasts can be reliable for some states and harmful in others, so reliability must be checked by regime.
concepts.aliases: seasonal skill limits, long-range forecast reliability
concepts.source_title: Weisheimer and Palmer, On the reliability of seasonal climate forecasts (ECMWF Tech Memo 722, 2014)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 5 to 1 scale, tropical temperature mostly category 4 or 5, dry Northern Europe summer rainfall category 1 verified.

concepts.name: GraphCast
concepts.def: A graph neural network weather model from Google DeepMind trained on reanalysis data that predicts hundreds of variables 10 days ahead at 0.25 degree resolution in under a minute. Its authors report it beats the leading operational deterministic system on 90% of 1380 verification targets. It is a single deterministic forecast, so it is exposed to the smoothing that RMSE-type scores reward and it gives no uncertainty estimate.
concepts.source_title: Lam et al., GraphCast: learning skillful medium-range global weather forecasting (arXiv 2212.12794)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 90% of 1380 targets, 0.25 degree, 10 days, under a minute, trained from reanalysis verified; GNN and DeepMind not stated in the abstract page.

concepts.name: GenCast
concepts.def: A diffusion-based machine-learning ensemble that generates stochastic 15-day global forecasts at 12-hour steps and 0.25 degree resolution in 8 minutes. Its authors report greater skill than ECMWF ENS on 97.4% of 1320 targets, scored with probabilistic metrics. It shows a learned generative model can produce calibrated ensembles, not only sharp point forecasts.
concepts.source_title: Price et al., GenCast: diffusion-based ensemble forecasting for medium-range weather (arXiv 2312.15796)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 15-day stochastic ensemble, 12-hour steps, 0.25 degree, 8 minutes, 97.4% of 1320 vs ENS verified; diffusion in title.

concepts.name: ECMWF AIFS
concepts.def: ECMWF's Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System, a graph neural network encoder and decoder around a sliding-window transformer processor, trained on ERA5 and operational analyses. The deterministic AIFS Single went operational on Feb 25, 2025 and the 51-member AIFS ENS on Jul 1, 2025, with ECMWF citing gains of up to 20% on some measures and about 1,000 times less energy per forecast. It marks the point where a leading forecaster runs ML and physics models side by side in operations.
concepts.aliases: aifs, aifs single, aifs ens, artificial intelligence forecasting system
concepts.source_title: Lang et al., AIFS: ECMWF's data-driven forecasting system (arXiv 2406.01465)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: GNN encoder/decoder with sliding-window transformer, ERA5 and operational analyses on arXiv page; operational dates, 51 members, 20% and 1,000x are from ECMWF nodes 29308 and 29407.

concepts.name: Smoothing bias of RMSE-trained forecasts
concepts.def: Deterministic scores such as RMSE reward forecasts that hedge toward the conditional mean, so models trained or judged on them become unrealistically smooth as uncertainty grows; WeatherBench 2 notes such scores heavily favor smooth forecasts. The ensemble mean scores well on RMSE but is not a realistic scenario. A return engine judged on point error alone will drift toward a flat forecast, which is why it is scored on the log score of a full distribution.
concepts.source_title: Rasp et al., WeatherBench 2: a benchmark for the next generation of data-driven global weather models
concepts.originator: Operational verification lore; documented in WeatherBench 2 (Rasp et al.), 2023
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: WeatherBench 2 says traditional scores heavily favor unrealistically smooth forecasts and ensemble mean is unrealistic but scores well.

concepts.name: CRPS decomposition
concepts.def: A split of the mean CRPS into miscalibration, discrimination and uncertainty components, the continuous counterpart of the Murphy Brier decomposition. Arnold, Walz, Ziegel and Gneiting propose an isotonicity-based version whose components are nonnegative. It tells a return engine whether a poor CRPS is a calibration problem (fixable) or a discrimination problem (no signal).
concepts.formula: mean CRPS = MSC - DSC + UNC
concepts.source_title: Arnold, Walz, Ziegel and Gneiting, Decompositions of the mean continuous ranked probability score (arXiv 2311.14122)
concepts.originator: Hersbach 2000; Arnold, Walz, Ziegel and Gneiting, 2023
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Isotonicity-based decomposition with nonnegative components verified; the paper abbreviates miscalibration as MSC, and Hersbach 2000 is not named on the page.

concepts.name: Palantir Ontology
concepts.def: An operational semantic layer that maps integrated datasets, models and virtual tables onto typed real-world objects, their properties and the links between them, plus the actions people may take on them. Palantir describes it as a digital twin of the organization. For a decision engine it is the reference design for a knowledge graph that is not only read but acted through, so every decision lands as a typed edit with lineage.
concepts.aliases: foundry ontology, operational ontology, semantic layer
concepts.source_title: Palantir Foundry documentation: Ontology overview
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Overview: operational layer on datasets, virtual tables and models, objects, links, actions, digital twin of the organization.

concepts.name: Ontology object type
concepts.def: The schema definition of a real-world entity or event, such as an aircraft, a patient, a company or a trade, with typed properties that describe its characteristics. Each row of backing data becomes an object instance. In an engine's knowledge graph the object type fixes what a node is, so that facts about the same thing do not scatter across duplicate nodes.
concepts.aliases: object type, entity type, node type
concepts.source_title: Palantir Foundry documentation: Ontology core concepts
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Core concepts: 'schema definition of a real-world entity or event', properties, objects as rows.

concepts.name: Ontology link type
concepts.def: The schema definition of a relationship between two object types, for example an employee linked to an employer or a supplier linked to a customer; many-to-many links carry their own backing data. Typed links are what make graph traversal and link analysis possible. For a market engine they encode exposures such as supplier, customer, competitor or hedge relations between holdings.
concepts.aliases: link type, relationship type, typed edge
concepts.source_title: Palantir Foundry documentation: Link types overview
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Link types page: schema definition of a relationship, Employee-Company example, many-to-many links backed by their own datasources.

concepts.name: Ontology action type
concepts.def: The schema definition of a set of edits to objects, property values and links that a user can take at once as a single transaction, with parameters, rules and side effects such as notifications. Actions turn a read-only model of the world into a system of record for decisions. For an OODA desk an action type is the typed form of the Act step: who may do what, with which inputs, and what gets logged.
concepts.aliases: action type, typed action, kinetic layer
concepts.source_title: Palantir Foundry documentation: Action types overview
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Action types page: set of edits as a single transaction with parameters, rules and side effects such as notifications.

concepts.name: Decision writeback
concepts.def: The practice of capturing each operator decision and edit as data in a writeback dataset attached to the objects it changed, rather than letting decisions vanish into email or memory. It closes the loop between analysis and action so outcomes can later be joined back to the decisions that caused them. A decision engine that writes back every sizing call can score its own judgment with proper scoring rules.
concepts.source_title: Palantir Foundry documentation: Action types overview
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Action types page says user edits are captured in an object type's writeback dataset; originator matches.

concepts.name: Palantir Foundry
concepts.def: Palantir's commercial data integration and operations platform, which it describes as an Ontology and AI powered operating system for the enterprise. It combines pipelines, lineage, the Ontology and applications so that integrated data can drive operational decisions. It is the platform behind documented cases such as Airbus Skywise and the NHS Federated Data Platform.
concepts.source_title: Palantir Foundry platform page
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page: 'Ontology/AI-powered operating system for the modern enterprise'; Skywise and NHS links are documented on other cited pages.

concepts.name: Palantir Gotham
concepts.def: Palantir's government and defense platform, which it calls the operating system for defense decision making. It fuses intelligence and sensor data into a shared picture for analysis, targeting and operations, and is the lineage of Palantir's link-analysis work for intelligence agencies. Its relevance for an engine is the pattern of fusing many noisy feeds into one decision surface under time pressure.

concepts.name: Digital twin
concepts.def: A continuously updated computational model of a physical system, product or organization, fed by real-time data and used for monitoring, prediction and simulation of what-if scenarios. The term is widely used loosely; a strict reading requires a live data link and a mechanism-based simulation. For a portfolio engine a twin of the book lets proposed actions be stressed before they are taken.

concepts.originator: engineering informatization practice; reviewed by Zhou, Zhang and Gu, 2022
