concepts.name: Decision intelligence
concepts.def: The discipline of modeling how actions lead to outcomes, typically with a diagram that places decision levers on one side, outcomes on the other and the causal chains between them. It treats data and models as inputs to a decision rather than ends in themselves. For a decision engine it argues for scoring the chain from signal to action to outcome, not only forecast accuracy.
concepts.source_title: Lorien Pratt, When artificial intelligence isn't enough: the new discipline of decision intelligence (Emerald, Mar 12, 2020)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Pratt (Emerald, Mar 12 2020): 'science and technology of understanding how actions lead to outcomes' with decision-to-outcome diagram; 2019 date not on page.

concepts.name: Decision support system
concepts.def: An interactive information system that supports human judgment on semi-structured decisions, where some phases (intelligence, design, choice) can be programmed and others cannot. Gorry and Scott Morton built the framework from Simon's programmed and nonprogrammed decisions and argued that interactive systems have their greatest potential in the semi-structured zone. It is the ancestor of the human-in-the-loop desk: the machine handles the structured parts, the human the rest.
concepts.source_title: Gorry and Scott Morton, A Framework for Management Information Systems (MIT Sloan WP 510-71, 1971)
concepts.originator: G. Anthony Gorry and Michael S. Scott Morton, 1971

concepts.name: Sensor-to-shooter timeline
concepts.def: The elapsed time from first detection of a target by any sensor to an effect on that target, the military measure that AI-enabled ground stations such as TITAN aim to shorten by fusing space, aerial and terrestrial data. It is the operational form of the OODA loop's speed. The market analog is signal-to-trade latency, which only matters when the signal decays faster than the decision cycle.
concepts.source_title: U.S. Army, TITAN Ground Station Prototype Award (Mar 6, 2024)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Army TITAN page uses 'reducing the sensor-to-shooter timeline' with space, high altitude, aerial and terrestrial sensor layers.

concepts.name: Federated data platform
concepts.def: An architecture in which each participating organization runs its own instance and remains controller of its own data, while shared software and common data models let insights and tools move between instances. It trades some analytical reach for trust, governance and adoption. For an engine that pulls many vendor feeds it argues for keeping each source separate with provenance rather than merging into one lake.
concepts.source_title: NHS England, NHS Federated Data Platform FAQs
concepts.originator: federated data architecture practice; NHS England's FDP (2023) as the reference case

concepts.def: An aviation data platform launched by Airbus in 2017 with Palantir that combines data from across the supply chain and from airline fleets into one data model for production, maintenance and reliability work. CIO reported more than 8,000 aircraft feeding data into the platform. It is the standard case of an ontology-backed platform creating value through supply chain visibility and predictive maintenance.

concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: CIO (Nov 8 2019): Palantir integrated supply chain data into a single model, more than 8,000 aircraft feed data; 2017 launch year not on page.

concepts.name: Fellegi-Sunter record linkage model
concepts.def: A probabilistic model for deciding whether two records refer to the same entity, using the ratio of the probability of an agreement pattern among true matches, m, to its probability among non-matches, u. Pairs are linked, not linked or sent for review, and the optimal rule minimizes the review share for fixed error rates. It is the statistical basis for merging aliases, tickers and renamed firms into one node in a knowledge graph.
concepts.formula: R(gamma) = m(gamma) / u(gamma); link (A1) if R >= T_mu, non-link (A3) if R <= T_lambda, possible link (A2) otherwise; mu = sum u(gamma) P(A1|gamma), lambda = sum m(gamma) P(A3|gamma)
concepts.aliases: probabilistic record linkage, fellegi-sunter, m and u probabilities
concepts.source_title: Fellegi and Sunter, A Theory for Record Linkage, JASA 64 (1969)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract supports m/u ratio decisions and minimizing P(A2); formula correct (mu = P(A1|U), lambda = P(A3|M), thresholds T_mu and T_lambda).

concepts.name: Possible-link review band
concepts.def: The middle decision zone in Fellegi-Sunter linkage where evidence is insufficient at the stated error levels, so the pair goes to clerical (human) review rather than an automatic link or non-link. Its width is set by the tolerated false-link and false-non-link rates. It generalizes into a design rule for any engine: automate the confident tails and route the ambiguous middle to a human.
concepts.aliases: clerical review zone, a2 possible link, abstain band
concepts.source_title: Fellegi and Sunter, A Theory for Record Linkage, JASA 64 (1969)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract defines possible link (A2) as failing a positive disposition, minimized at fixed error levels; clerical review is the paper's framing.

concepts.name: Link analysis
concepts.def: Investigating entities through the network of relationships among them, such as shared directors, addresses, accounts or counterparties, rather than through each entity's own attributes. Graph queries such as everyone within two degrees of a person expose rings and hidden common owners, as in the ICIJ Panama Papers work. For a market engine it reveals shared exposures across holdings, for example one supplier behind several AI names.
concepts.aliases: network analysis, graph analytics, relationship analysis
concepts.source_title: ICIJ, Wrangling 2.6TB of data: The people and the technology behind the Panama Papers (Apr 25, 2016)
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: ICIJ page supports two-degree graph queries over people, companies and addresses with Neo4j and Linkurious; title is wrong.

concepts.name: Graph-based anomaly detection
concepts.def: Methods that find unusual nodes, edges, subgraphs or changes in graph data, where objects are correlated through their links, and that attribute the anomaly to a root cause. Applications include financial fraud, auction fraud, network traffic and social networks. For a knowledge graph it flags concepts or entities whose link patterns suddenly change.
concepts.aliases: graph anomaly detection, network anomaly detection
concepts.source_title: Akoglu, Tong and Koutra, Graph-based Anomaly Detection and Description: A Survey (arXiv 2014)
concepts.originator: Leman Akoglu, Hanghang Tong and Danai Koutra, 2014 (survey)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Akoglu, Tong and Koutra survey (Apr 2014) covers graph anomalies, attribution and applications in finance, auctions, traffic and social networks.

concepts.name: Anomaly detection
concepts.def: Identifying observations that do not conform to the bulk of the data, either by profiling normal behavior and flagging departures or by isolating rare points directly, as isolation forests do. It is unsupervised or weakly supervised because labeled anomalies are rare. In a market engine it flags months or data points that are unlike the training history, where model outputs deserve less trust.
concepts.source_title: Liu, Ting and Zhou, Isolation Forest (ICDM 2008)
concepts.originator: statistics and data mining; isolation approach by Liu, Ting and Zhou, 2008
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Isolation Forest paper contrasts profiling normal points with isolating anomalies; originator line fits.

concepts.name: Changepoint detection
concepts.def: Detecting abrupt changes in the parameters of the process that generates a sequence, either retrospectively (segmentation) or online as data arrive. Online detection matters in finance because a model fitted before a break keeps issuing confident but stale forecasts. It complements CUSUM tests and regime models.
concepts.aliases: change point detection, structural break detection, change detection
concepts.source_title: Adams and MacKay, Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection (arXiv 2007)
concepts.originator: statistical process control tradition; online Bayesian form by Adams and MacKay, 2007
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Adams and MacKay abstract defines changepoints as abrupt variations in generative parameters and contrasts online with retrospective segmentation.

concepts.name: Bayesian online changepoint detection
concepts.def: An exact online algorithm that maintains a posterior over the run length, the time since the last changepoint, updating it with a message-passing recursion as each observation arrives. A hazard function sets the prior chance of a break each step. It gives a probability that a regime just ended, which a sizing rule can use directly.
concepts.source_title: Adams and MacKay, Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection (2007), ar5iv rendering
concepts.originator: Ryan P. Adams and David J. C. MacKay, 2007
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Formula matches Algorithm 1 steps 4 and 5 exactly, with H(tau)=1/lambda for constant hazard.

concepts.name: Collaborative filtering
concepts.def: Predicting a user's preference for an item from the preferences of similar users or the ratings of similar items, without content features. Its weakness is the cold start problem for new users and items. In a research engine the same idea scores how a rule or signal will behave in a new period from its behavior in similar past periods.
concepts.source_title: Koren, Bell and Volinsky, Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems, IEEE Computer (Aug 2009)
concepts.originator: Goldberg et al. (Tapestry, 1992); popularized by the Netflix Prize
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Koren et al. describe CF, its cold start weakness and credit Tapestry (Goldberg et al.) with coining the term.

concepts.name: Matrix factorization for recommendation
concepts.def: A latent factor model that represents each user and item as a vector and predicts a rating as a global mean plus user and item biases plus the dot product of the vectors, fitted by regularized least squares on observed ratings only. It was the core of the leading Netflix Prize entries. Applied to a months by signals performance matrix it can uncover latent regimes and fill untested cells.
concepts.formula: r_hat_ui = mu + b_i + b_u + q_i' p_u; minimize sum_(u,i observed) (r_ui - mu - b_u - b_i - p_u' q_i)^2 + lambda (||p_u||^2 + ||q_i||^2 + b_u^2 + b_i^2)
concepts.aliases: latent factor model, svd recommender, funk svd
concepts.source_title: Koren, Bell and Volinsky, Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems, IEEE Computer (Aug 2009)
concepts.originator: Yehuda Koren, Robert Bell and Chris Volinsky, 2009
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Formula matches Eqs. 4 and 5; paper says winning Netflix Prize entries were mostly factorization models.

concepts.name: Cold start problem
concepts.def: The failure of collaborative methods to make good predictions for new users or items that have little or no history. Remedies borrow strength from content features, priors or similar entities. A market engine faces it with new tickers such as recent listings, where the right default is a prior from comparable firms and wide uncertainty.
concepts.source_title: Koren, Bell and Volinsky, Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems, IEEE Computer (Aug 2009)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Paper: 'collaborative filtering suffers from what is called the cold start problem' for new products and users.

concepts.name: Offline accuracy versus deployment value
concepts.def: The gap between a gain measured offline on a fixed benchmark and the value it creates once engineering cost, latency and changing use are counted. Netflix paid 1 million dollars for the Prize yet judged that the extra accuracy of the final ensemble did not justify the engineering effort, partly because its focus had moved on after the 2007 launch of streaming. A decision engine should price model complexity against decision value, not against benchmark error.
concepts.aliases: benchmark-to-production gap, accuracy is not value
concepts.source_title: Amatriain and Basilico, Netflix Recommendations: Beyond the 5 stars (Part 1), Netflix Tech Blog (Apr 6, 2012)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Blog supports $1 million prize, Grand Prize gains not justifying engineering effort, and focus shifting after 2007 streaming launch.

concepts.name: Netflix Prize
concepts.def: A public competition, 2006 to 2009, offering 1 million dollars to whoever improved the accuracy of Netflix's Cinematch rating predictor by 10%; BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos won in 2009. It advanced matrix factorization and ensembling, but the final blend was never fully deployed and the released data were shown to be re-identifiable. It is a case study in both the value and the limits of leaderboard science.
concepts.source_title: Amatriain and Basilico, Netflix Recommendations: Beyond the 5 stars (Part 1), Netflix Tech Blog (Apr 6, 2012)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Blog confirms 2006 start, $1 million for 10% over Cinematch and non-deployment of the final blend; the BellKor winner name and re-identification come from elsewhere.

concepts.name: Re-identification risk
concepts.def: The risk that records released as anonymous can be linked back to individuals using a little outside knowledge, because high-dimensional data such as ratings or transactions are nearly unique per person. Narayanan and Shmatikov did this to the Netflix Prize data using IMDb. For alternative data it is both a compliance risk and a reminder that panel data carry personal fingerprints.
concepts.source_title: Narayanan and Shmatikov, How To Break Anonymity of the Netflix Prize Dataset (arXiv 2006)
concepts.originator: Arvind Narayanan and Vitaly Shmatikov, 2006, for high-dimensional data (earlier re-identification work by Latanya Sweeney)
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Abstract supports the Netflix re-identification with IMDb; the general re-identification concept predates them, so originator is too broad.

concepts.name: Adaptive leaderboard overfitting
concepts.def: Overfitting to a reused holdout set when many submissions are scored against it and participants adapt to the public score. Blum and Hardt's Ladder limits it by revealing a new best score only when a submission beats the previous best by a margin. A meta-analysis of over one hundred Kaggle competitions found little substantial overfitting, so the risk is real but often smaller than feared when the holdout is large.
concepts.aliases: test set reuse, adaptive overfitting, the ladder
concepts.source_title: Blum and Hardt, The Ladder: A Reliable Leaderboard for Machine Learning Competitions (arXiv 2015)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Ladder paper addresses holdout overfitting in competitions with a margin-based release rule (Figure 1); Kaggle meta-analysis figure matches Roelofs.

concepts.name: Credit scorecard
concepts.def: A points-based model, usually logistic regression on binned and weight-of-evidence transformed variables, that converts applicant characteristics into a score ranking default risk. Scorecards are valued for monotonic, explainable bins and stable performance more than raw accuracy. Their discipline (binning, monotonicity, population stability checks) transfers to any engine that must explain why it changed exposure.
concepts.aliases: application scorecard, behavioral scorecard, points scorecard
concepts.source_title: scorecardmodel documentation: Weight of Evidence (WOE), In-Depth Guide
concepts.originator: consumer credit industry, Fair Isaac and others from the 1950s
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: scorecardmodel guide presents WoE-based scorecards with logistic regression, monotonic bins and regulatory explainability; Fair Isaac history is not on page.

concepts.name: Weight of evidence
concepts.def: For each bin of a variable, the log of the share of goods in that bin over the share of bads, so positive values favor good outcomes and negative values favor bad ones. It linearizes the variable for logistic regression and handles missing values as their own bin. It is the same log likelihood ratio that Fellegi-Sunter and Bayesian updating use, which makes it a natural unit for an evidence gate.
concepts.formula: WoE_i = ln(dist_good_i / dist_bad_i)
concepts.source_title: R package scorecard: iv documentation
concepts.originator: I. J. Good (weight of evidence, 1950); credit scoring practice
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: R iv page gives WoE = ln(DistPositive/DistNegative); concept's good/bad orientation is a standard convention and the formula is correct. Good 1950 originator fits.

concepts.name: Information value
concepts.def: A summary of a variable's predictive strength in a scorecard, summing over bins the difference in good and bad shares times the weight of evidence. Common thresholds call values below 0.02 useless, 0.1 to 0.3 medium and above 0.3 strong, and practitioners treat values above 0.5 as suspicious for leakage. That last convention is a cheap leakage alarm for any feature a market model adds.
concepts.formula: IV = sum_i (dist_good_i - dist_bad_i) * ln(dist_good_i / dist_bad_i)
concepts.source_title: scorecardmodel documentation: Weight of Evidence (WOE), In-Depth Guide
concepts.checked: corrected by a second checker: Formula correct and R page gives 0.02/0.1/0.3 thresholds, but the 0.5 leakage convention is only on the scorecardmodel guide, which lists all thresholds.

concepts.name: Reject inference
concepts.def: Techniques that correct a credit model for the fact that repayment outcomes are only observed for applicants who were accepted, by inferring or reweighting the outcomes of rejects so the model reflects the full through-the-door population. Ignoring it biases the model toward the population past policy chose. Any engine that learns only from trades it took faces the same selection problem.
concepts.source_title: Etimova, Gregory and Marcheva, An Empirical Survey of Reject Inference Techniques (Credit Scoring and Credit Control XIII, Aug 2013)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Survey (CSCC XIII, Aug 2013) describes known-performance bias from ignoring rejects and reweighting to the through-the-door population; authors and venue match.

concepts.name: FICO Score
concepts.def: The standard US consumer credit risk score, built from five categories of credit report data weighted roughly as payment history 35%, amounts owed 30%, length of credit history 15%, new credit 10% and credit mix 10%. It is the canonical example of a stable, explainable, widely adopted risk score. Its lesson for an engine is that a few robust, slow-moving inputs can beat many fragile ones.
concepts.source_title: myFICO, What's in my FICO Scores?
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: myFICO lists the five categories and weights; the 1956 founding year is not on the page but is correct.

concepts.name: Usage-based insurance
concepts.def: Auto insurance priced on telematics data about how, when and how much a policyholder drives, such as hard braking, speed and mileage, rather than only on static rating factors. Monitoring also changes behavior: a Marketing Science study found drivers cut daily hard brakes by an average of 21 percent after six months. It shows a feedback loop where the measurement alters the risk it measures.
concepts.source_title: INFORMS, When the insurance company monitors your driving in real time, does it help? (Feb 6, 2019)
concepts.originator: insurance industry; studied by Soleymanian, Weinberg and Zhu, 2019
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: INFORMS release: telematics UBI, 21 percent fewer hard brakes after six months, Marketing Science, Feb 6 2019.

concepts.name: Telematics data
concepts.def: Sensor streams from vehicles or devices recording location, speed, acceleration and braking, used by insurers to observe risk directly instead of inferring it from proxies. Direct observation reduces adverse selection because low-risk drivers can prove they are low risk. It is a template for alternative data that measures behavior rather than reported outcomes.
concepts.source_title: INFORMS, When the insurance company monitors your driving in real time, does it help? (Feb 6, 2019)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Release describes telematics monitoring of miles, time, location, acceleration and braking; the adverse-selection sentence is general reasoning not on the page.

concepts.name: Alert false-positive burden
concepts.def: The operational cost created when a monitoring system flags far more cases than are real, as in bank anti-money-laundering transaction monitoring where false-positive rates of roughly 90% to 95% are commonly reported. Reviewers then tune out alerts and the rare true case is missed. Any engine that raises warnings must track precision, not only recall, and cap its alert rate.
concepts.source_title: Columbia SIPA, Detecting Financial Crimes: Evaluating the Efficacy of Automated Transaction Monitoring
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Columbia SIPA paper: TMS false-positive rates 'approximately 90%-95% on average' with high operational overhead and missed high-value alerts.

concepts.name: Ensemble spread as uncertainty
concepts.def: In ensemble weather prediction, many forecasts are run from slightly perturbed initial conditions and model physics, and the spread of their results measures forecast uncertainty: the greater the spread, the less certain the forecast. ECMWF runs 51 members at about 9 km resolution. For a market engine the dispersion across its forecasters is a free, checkable uncertainty signal, if spread and error are shown to move together.
concepts.source_title: ECMWF, Medium-range forecasts documentation
concepts.originator: ECMWF and NCEP ensemble prediction systems, 1992
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: ECMWF: 51 members at about 9 km, perturbed initial conditions and physics, greater spread means greater uncertainty; 1992 date not on page but correct.

concepts.name: Effective reproduction number (Rt)
concepts.def: The average number of secondary cases each case generates at time t, estimated as new incidence divided by total infectiousness, the sum of past incidence weighted by the serial interval distribution. Cori and coauthors estimate it over a sliding window with a gamma prior, giving an analytic posterior. It is a growth ratio with a known lag structure, which is how a nowcast should treat any self-reinforcing series.
concepts.formula: R_t = I_t / Lambda_t; Lambda_t = sum_{s=1..t} w_s * I_{t-s}
concepts.source_title: Cori, Ferguson, Fraser and Cauchemez, A New Framework and Software to Estimate Time-Varying Reproduction Numbers During Epidemics, AJE 178(9) (2013)
concepts.originator: Anne Cori et al., 2013 (instantaneous form after Fraser, 2007)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Cori et al. define R_t as incidence over total infectiousness with gamma prior; Lambda_t = sum_{s=1..t} w_s I_{t-s} is the paper's formula.

concepts.name: Google Flu Trends
concepts.def: A 2008 to 2015 Google service that estimated weekly influenza-like illness from search query volumes, claiming a reporting lag of about one day. It later overestimated flu badly in 2012 and 2013 and Google stopped publishing it in 2015. It is the canonical big data nowcasting failure: correlation mined from a vast pool of search terms, no structural model, and an input stream that the provider kept changing.
concepts.source_title: Ginsberg et al., Detecting influenza epidemics using search engine query data, Nature 457 (2009)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Ginsberg page supports the method and one-day lag; the 2015 shutdown is correct but not on this page.

concepts.name: Big data hubris
concepts.def: Lazer and coauthors' term for the often implicit assumption that big data are a substitute for, rather than a supplement to, traditional data collection and analysis. Volume does not fix measurement, construct validity or dependence between data points. For a research engine it means alternative feeds should be blended with and recalibrated against slower ground truth, never replace it.
concepts.source_title: Lazer, Kennedy, King and Vespignani, The Parable of Google Flu: Traps in Big Data Analysis, Science 343 (2014)
concepts.originator: David Lazer, Ryan Kennedy, Gary King and Alessandro Vespignani, 2014
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Lazer et al. define it verbatim as the assumption that big data substitute for traditional data collection and analysis.

concepts.name: Algorithm dynamics
concepts.def: Changes in a data-generating platform made by its engineers to improve the commercial service, together with changes in user behavior, that silently alter what a big data series measures. Changes to Google search are a leading suspect in Google Flu Trends' overestimates. Any alternative data feed produced by a platform for another purpose carries this risk, so its meaning must be re-validated over time.
concepts.source_title: Lazer, Kennedy, King and Vespignani, The Parable of Google Flu: Traps in Big Data Analysis, Science 343 (2014)
concepts.originator: David Lazer, Ryan Kennedy, Gary King and Alessandro Vespignani, 2014
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Lazer et al.: 'Algorithm dynamics are the changes made by engineers to improve the commercial service' plus user behavior changes.

concepts.name: Lagged ground-truth recalibration
concepts.def: Combining a fast but noisy big data signal with the slower authoritative series it proxies, using the latest available official values as inputs and refitting the mapping as new truth arrives. Lazer and coauthors showed that combining Google Flu Trends with lagged CDC data and dynamic recalibration substantially beat either alone. It is the standard fix for any nowcast built on alternative data.
concepts.aliases: nowcast recalibration, blend with lagged truth
concepts.source_title: Lazer, Kennedy, King and Vespignani, The Parable of Google Flu: Traps in Big Data Analysis, Science 343 (2014)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Paper says combining GFT and lagged CDC data with dynamic recalibration substantially improves on GFT or CDC alone.

concepts.name: Pythagorean expectation
concepts.def: Bill James's estimate of a team's underlying winning percentage from runs scored and allowed, which predicts future records better than the actual record because close-game luck regresses away. Miller derived it from Weibull-distributed scoring and found an exponent near 1.8. The market analog is judging a price move against the fundamentals that should drive it and expecting the gap to close.
concepts.formula: W% = RS^c / (RS^c + RA^c), c about 1.82 for baseball
concepts.source_title: Steven J. Miller, A Derivation of the Pythagorean Won-Loss Formula in Baseball (arXiv 2005)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Miller's abstract credits Bill James, uses Weibull scoring, fits c = 1.79 and 1.74 vs observed 1.82; formula correct.

concepts.name: Sabermetrics
concepts.def: Bill James's term for the search for objective knowledge about baseball, the use of statistical evidence to test received wisdom about which skills win games. It found that conventional scouting mispriced some skills, such as getting on base. For an investor it is the model of an edge that comes from measuring the right thing better than incumbents, and that decays once rivals copy it.
concepts.source_title: SABR, A Guide to Sabermetric Research
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SABR: Bill James defined it in 1980 as 'the search for objective knowledge about baseball'; mispriced on-base skill comes from Hakes and Sauer, not this page.

concepts.name: Moneyball mispricing
concepts.def: The finding that the baseball labor market undervalued certain skills early in the 1999 to 2004 period, letting statistically minded teams buy wins cheaply, and that the mispricing was corrected as knowledge spread to other teams. Hakes and Sauer showed it with standard econometrics on pay and productivity. It is a clean natural experiment in how a data edge earns a premium and then decays after publication.
concepts.source_title: Hakes and Sauer, An Economic Evaluation of the Moneyball Hypothesis, JEP 20(3) (2006)
concepts.originator: Michael Lewis (Moneyball, 2003); tested by Jahn Hakes and Raymond Sauer, 2006
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: JEP abstract supports 1999-2004 undervaluation, profitable exploitation and correction as knowledge dispersed.

concepts.name: Satellite parking-lot signal
concepts.def: Counting cars in retailers' parking lots from satellite images to estimate store traffic and sales ahead of earnings reports. Katona, Painter, Patatoukas and Zeng used 4.8 million images of lots at 67,000 stores of 44 retailers and found a strategy earning 4% to 5% in the three days around announcements. The edge accrued to sophisticated short sellers, with individual investors on the other side.
concepts.source_title: Berkeley Haas Newsroom, How hedge funds use satellite images to beat Wall Street and Main Street (May 28, 2019)
concepts.originator: Zsolt Katona, Marcus Painter, Panos Patatoukas and Jean Zeng
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Haas article: 4.8 million images, 67,000 stores, 44 retailers, 4% to 5% over three days; four coauthors named.

concepts.name: Unequal access to big data
concepts.def: When costly alternative data reach only some investors, they can raise information asymmetry and lower liquidity around news without immediately improving price discovery. Katona and coauthors found more informed short selling and less informed individual buying around reports of satellite-covered retailers. A model book that does not buy such data should assume the other side of event trades is better informed.
concepts.source_title: Katona, Painter, Patatoukas and Zeng, On the Capital Market Consequences of Big Data: Evidence from Outer Space, JFQA 60(2) (2025)
concepts.originator: Zsolt Katona, Marcus Painter, Panos Patatoukas and Jean Zeng, 2025
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: JFQA abstract quotes on informed short selling, lower liquidity and asymmetry without immediate price discovery confirmed.

concepts.name: Real-time sales proxy
concepts.def: An estimate of a company's current-quarter revenue built from consumer activity data, such as location signals from tens of millions of mobile devices, before the company reports. Froot, Kang, Ozik and Sadka found the within-quarter proxy explains sales growth and earnings surprises and is associated with average excess returns of 3.4% at announcement. It is the firm-level version of nowcasting.
concepts.source_title: Froot, Kang, Ozik and Sadka, What Do Measures of Real-time Corporate Sales Tell Us about Earnings Surprises and Post-Announcement Returns? (NBER WP 22366, 2016)
concepts.originator: Kenneth Froot, Namho Kang, Gideon Ozik and Ronnie Sadka, 2016
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER abstract: ~50 million mobile devices, explains sales growth and surprises, 3.4% excess return at announcement.

concepts.name: Renaissance Medallion fund
concepts.def: Renaissance Technologies' internal quantitative fund, whose reported returns from 1988 through 2018 compound to 63.3% a year with no negative year over 31 years and negative market beta, by Cornell's reconstruction. It is the strongest documented case that large-scale data and statistical modeling can earn persistent excess returns. Its capacity limits and secrecy also show why such edges are not available to outside capital.
concepts.source_title: Bradford Cornell, Medallion Fund: The Ultimate Counterexample? (SSRN 2020; JPM 46(4))
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Cornell abstract: 63.3% compound return 1988-2018, no negative year over 31 years, negative beta and factor loadings.

concepts.name: Two Sigma
concepts.def: A quantitative investment firm founded in 2001 by David Siegel, John Overdeck and Mark Pickard on the premise that technology and data science can discover value in the world's data. With Renaissance it is the archetype of an asset manager organized as a data and research firm, where edge comes from data acquisition, infrastructure and research process rather than individual stock picking. The lesson is that the process, not any single signal, is the durable asset.
concepts.source_title: Two Sigma, About
concepts.originator: David Siegel, John Overdeck and Mark Pickard, 2001
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: About page: founded 2001 by David Siegel, John Overdeck and Mark Pickard on the belief that technology and data science can discover value in the world's data.

concepts.name: Zillow Offers wind-down (2021)
concepts.def: Zillow's algorithmic home-buying business, closed in Nov 2021 after a 304.4 million dollar inventory write-down for the third quarter, with about a 25% cut in staff; the board cited home pricing unpredictability, capacity constraints and operational challenges. A price model that was good enough to advise became ruinous when the firm acted on it at scale with its own balance sheet. It is the clearest case of a decision platform failing when forecast error met leverage, adverse selection and a turning market.
concepts.source_title: Zillow Group, Form 8-K (Nov 2, 2021)
concepts.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 8-K: Nov 2 2021 wind-down decision, $304.4 million Q3 write-down, about 25% workforce cut, cited causes match; 'closed' means wound down from that date.

concepts.name: Deduction
concepts.def: Reasoning from premises to a conclusion that must be true if the premises are. The engine deduces with typed rules (transitivity, inheritance, causal composition with signs) and keeps a proof for every derived fact, so a conclusion can be traced and challenged.
concepts.formula: premises P1..Pn, rule (P1 and ... and Pn) implies C; C follows
concepts.checked: written by the lead agent for the reasoning engine (v0.25)

concepts.name: Induction from data
concepts.def: Reasoning from observed cases to a general rule. Unlike deduction it can be wrong, so the engine finds rules on one period, tests them on a later one it never saw, and corrects for how many it tried.
concepts.formula: effect = mean(Y | C) - mean(Y | not C), tested out of sample
concepts.checked: written by the lead agent for the reasoning engine (v0.25)

concepts.name: Abduction
concepts.def: Inference to the best explanation: given an outcome, rank the conditions that most raise its likelihood. It proposes hypotheses; it does not prove them, and on the site it is labelled retrospective.
concepts.formula: LR(h) = P(obs | h) / P(obs | not h); rank by P(h | obs) - P(h)
concepts.aliases: inference to the best explanation, abductive reasoning
concepts.checked: written by the lead agent for the reasoning engine (v0.25)

concepts.name: Reasoning mode
concepts.def: The kind of inference a system makes: deduction (what must follow), induction (what usually holds), abduction (what best explains) and invention (what new concept would help). Each needs its own test.
concepts.checked: written by the lead agent for the reasoning engine (v0.25)

concepts.name: Concept invention
concepts.def: Proposing a new concept from data, such as a regime found by a mixture model or a predicate built from two features, and keeping it only if it forecasts better out of sample than what it replaces.
concepts.formula: choose K by BIC; score membership by out-of-sample skill
concepts.aliases: predicate invention, latent concept, regime discovery
concepts.checked: written by the lead agent for the reasoning engine (v0.25)

concepts.name: Forward chaining
concepts.def: Deduction that starts from known facts and applies every rule whose conditions hold, adding the conclusions, until nothing new follows (a fixpoint). Semi-naive evaluation reapplies rules only to facts new in the last round.
concepts.formula: repeat: add head for every rule whose body is satisfied, until no change
concepts.checked: written by the lead agent for the reasoning engine (v0.25)

concepts.name: Horn clause
concepts.def: A rule with one conclusion and a conjunction of conditions, if A and B then C. Sets of Horn clauses can be evaluated to a unique fixpoint efficiently, which is why the engine writes its policy and its graph rules in this form.
concepts.formula: (B1 and ... and Bn) implies H
concepts.checked: written by the lead agent for the reasoning engine (v0.25)
